stem: A man owes his friend £80 to be paid on by 1 May. The man gives his friend an MP3 player worth £15 on 30 April in full satisfaction of the debt.
ask: Which of the following statements best advises the parties with regard to promissory?

The creditor will not be able to recover the balance of the debt if the payment of £15 on the due date is paid in good faith by the debtor
If the debtor provides goods or services instead of cash, this will discharge the debt fully, because the gift of a 'horse, hawk or robe' may be more beneficial than the money
The payment of goods valued at £15 on the due date can never discharge a debt of £80
Since the debtor had paid early, he has provided sufficient consideration to discharge the whole debt

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. While the payment of £15 on the due date could never discharge a debt of £80, if the debtor offered and the creditor accepted an MP3 player worth £15 in satisfaction, the creditor could not then claim the balance of £65. • me mus use sure nose musiarge a debt

stem: Your client has been criminally charged with false imprisonment. He is also being pursued through the civil courts for the same reason. He understands that he is the defendant but confused as to which parties bring civil and criminal cases.

stem: Client A instructs you that a sum of £400.00 held by you in a designated deposit account on his behalf should be considered as client B's money.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: Transfer £400.00 from client A's designated deposit account to the general client account: Debit cash sheet Credit client A's designated deposit ledger client account (£400.00) Then transfer £400.00 to client B's ledger account: Debit client B's ledger Credit cash sheet client account (£400.00)
Transfer £400.00 in the general client account from client A's ledger account to • client B's ledger account: Credit client A's ledger Debit client B's ledger client account (£400.00)

Provided you obtain written authority from client A, you only need to make a 'paper transfer' to re-designate the funds: Debit client A's designated deposit ledger Credit client B's ledger client account (£400.00)

Transfer £400.00 from client A's designated deposit account to the general client account: Debit cash sheet Credit client A's designated deposit ledger client account (£400.00) Memorandum entry in client A's ledger account. Do a 'paper transfer' of £400.00 in the general client account from client A's ledger account to client B's ledger account: Debit client A's ledger Credit client B's ledger client account (£400.00)

Transfer the money from client A's designated deposit account to the office account, recorded on client B's ledger account: Debit client A's ledger Credit client A's designated deposit ledger client account (£400.00) Debit cash sheet office account Credit client B's ledger client account (£400.00)

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. First, you need to record the transfer of the money from client's A designated account into the general client account. Then, reflect the transfer of the money from client A to client B. No double entry records are required for the cash accounts in this case since money is not paid out of one account nor paid into a different account. However, you must record the 'transfer' of money in the transfer journal, giving details on the date of the transfer, the sum transferred and the reason why the transfer was made. The transfer is actually from client A's ledger account to client B's ledger account. This kind of transfer is called a 'paper transfer' or a 'client ledger transfer' (Rule 27). A is wrong, because you do not need to, nor do you have instruction to, withdraw the entirety of the money held in client A's separate designated client account to effect the transfer. Nor is there a paper transfer of £400.00 once the transfer has been made. B is wrong, because the money is to be transferred from client A's separate designated client account; it is not held in the general client account already. C is wrong, because the 'paper transfer' here attempts to designate money held in a separate client account as belonging to client B in the general client account. This would be a breach of Rules 1 and 29. There is no requirement to obtain written authority for a paper transfer, unless the transfer is in respect of private loans - Rule 27 (2). E is wrong because money from the designated deposit account cannot be used as a payment to another client per Rule 20(8). According to Rule 27 a 'paper transfer' may only be made if it would have been permissible to withdraw that sum from client A's account (under Rule 20(1)) and also would have been permissible to pay that sum into client B's account (under Rule 14). E is also wrong since one entry is made in the office account and the other in the client account. This is always incorrect.

stem: It was not until the famous case of Donoghue v Stevenson that a general principle was firmly established for determining the existence of a duty of care. Before that time, the tort was applied to damage caused in very specific circumstances where the courts decided that a duty ought to be owed, e.g. road accidents, but it was a principle of general application.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes a party's duty to his neighbour under the law of tort?

options.en: A party has a duty towards a specific individual
A party has a duty towards a group of individuals
A party has a duty towards the world at large
A party has a duty towards a specific individual and towards a group of individuals
A party has a duty towards a specific individual, a group of individuals and towards the world at large

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. A defendant owes a duty to "...persons who are so closely and directly affected by my act that I ought reasonably to have them in contemplation as being so affected when I am directing my mind to the acts or omissions which are called in question...". One of the main concerns, however, is the 'floodgates' argument - without any form of control mechanism, "a negligent defendant might find himself being made liable to all the world" (Page v Smith). Lead case: Donoghue v Stevenson [1932].

stem: A woman has been arrested for allegedly stealing a dress from a ladies fashion store. You are called to the police station to advise her prior to police interview. She is unsure of the mens rea of the offence of theft - i.e. the thought pattern behind the crime - and asks for an explanation.
ask: Which of the following statements best defines the mens rea of the offence of theft?

options.en: The mens rea of the offence of theft is usually defined as dishonesty with the intention to permanently deprive property belonging to another
The mens rea of the offence of theft is usually defined as the dishonest appropriation of property with the intention to permanently deprive
The mens rea of the offence of theft is usually defined as the appropriation of property with the intention to permanently deprive
The mens rea of the offence of theft is usually defined as dishonesty with the intention to deprive
The mens rea of the offence of theft is usually defined as dishonesty with the intention to permanently deprive

explanation.en: E is correct. The mens rea of the offence of theft is usually defined as dishonesty with the intention to permanently deprive. While this is clear, the definition of each term and their relationship with each other is less so, due to the uncertainty behind appropriation and the over reliance on the dishonesty element to secure a conviction.

stem: This doctrine invokes a Member State's residual power, whereby the jurisprudence of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) defers to the Member State when it weighs legitimate justifications for rights infringements under the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention). The question for the ECtHR is whether the state has correctly balanced its own interests with the Convention rights of the individual.
ask: To which doctrine does the statement refer?

options.en: The doctrine of incorporation
The doctrine of transformation
The doctrine of judicial review
The doctrine of positive obligation
The doctrine of the margin of appreciation

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. E is correct. Contracting States are allowed a margin of appreciation; that is to say, they may restrict Convention rights, based on the political, social and cultural traditions with which they are more closely attuned than is the ECtHR. Lead case: Handyside v. United Kingdom [1976] 1 EHRR 737.

stem: A private limited company is seeking a loan from the bank, but the bank has advised that its director needs to provide a personal guarantee. The director is not aware that directors are allowed to provide personal guarantees and would like further clarification.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the situation?

options.en: Directors cannot provide personal guarantees in any situation
Directors can only provide personal guarantees when the sum involved is less than £100,000
Directors can only provide personal guarantees when the sum involved exceeds £100,000
Directors can only provide personal guarantees when the sum involved is less than £250,000
Directors may be required to give a personal guarantee

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Sometimes, when entering into a contract (e.g. obtaining a loan) the lender will require a personal guarantee of a director. This may take the form of a charge over the director's house etc.

stem: A freehold owner of a large townhouse in central London executes an inter vivos declaration of trust under hand, in which she transfers the property to her trustees to be held on trust for a beneficiary until the beneficiary reaches the age of 21, with that beneficiary and her mother being given a right to occupy the property until that time. The settlor does not execute a transfer of the legal title to the land. She subsequently argues with the beneficiary's mother and decides that she no longer wishes the property to be subject to the trust. Which of the following statements best describes the position? be neid on trust tor a beneticiary until the beneticiary reaches the age of 21, with that beneficiary and her mother being given a right to occupy the property until that time. The settlor does not execute a transfer of the legal title to the land. She subsequently argues with the beneficiary's mother and decides that she no longer wishes the property to be subject to the trust.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The property was subject to the trust from the date that the settlor executed the trust instrument and she is unable to revoke this
The property was subject to the trust from the date that the settlor executed • the trust instrument, but the settlor can apply to the court for the trust to be revoked
The property is not subject to a trust, but the beneficiary could apply to the • court for an order for specific performance, compelling the settlor to transfer the land to the trustees
The property is not subject to a trust

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. In order to render a voluntary settlement valid and effectual, the settlor must have done everything which was necessary to be done in order to transfer the property and render the settlement binding upon herself. In the case of land, the disposition must be made by deed to transfer an equitable interest. The maxim that "equity will not perfect an imperfect gift" would apply and an order for specific performance would be unavailable.

stem: A man who had been drinking heavily mistakenly went 'home' to the wrong house. Failing to make the key work, he smashed the glass in the front door and let himself in. Once inside, the man realised that he was in the wrong house, and on his way out picked up an umbrella that was in the hallway, because it had started to rain outside. Which of the following best states at what point, if at all, the man became criminally liable for burglary? Falling to make the key work, he smashed the glass in the tront door and let himselt in. Once inside, the man realised that he was in the wrong house, and on his way out picked up an umbrella that was in the hallway, because it had started to rain outside.
ask: Which of the following best states at what point, if at all, the man became criminally liable for burglary?

options.en: The point at which the man became criminally liable for burglary was when he smashed the glass in the front door
The point at which the man became criminally liable for burglary was when he let himself into the house

, The man cannot be criminally liable, because voluntary intoxication provides a defence for a crime of specific intent

stem: You act for an offshore registered investment company. You provide legal advice on a series of transactions that later turn out to have been used to finance money laundering. You did not directly facilitate or become involved in the transactions themselves. You believed at the time that the advice was to further a legitimate purpose. Accordingly, no disclosure was made.
ask: Which of the following best describes?

options.en: You have committed both 'arranging' and 'failure to disclose' offences, and have no defence to either
You may have committed a 'failure to disclose' offence, but can rely on the 'reasonable excuse' defence, as you were misled
You may have committed both 'arranging' and 'failure to disclose' offences, but can rely on the 'reasonable excuse' defence for both offences
You have not committed any offences
You may have committed an 'arranging' offence, but can rely on the 'reasonable excuse' defence

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. You have not committed an 'arranging' offence as this requires you to have been either a party to it or taken steps to put it into effect, beyond merely advising. The Law Society's view, expressed in paragraph 5.4.3 of their Practice Note on anti-money laundering, states that entering into or becoming concerned in an arrangement involves an act done at a particular time; an offence is only committed once the arrangement is actually made, and preparatory or intermediate steps in transactional work which does not itself involve the acquisition, retention, use or control of property will not constitute the making of an arrangement under s328. Where matters giving rise to suspicion come to a professional legal adviser in privileged circumstances (which is the case here), and the crime/fraud exemption does not apply, then the solicitor will be prevented from making a disclosure. However, you have inadvertently given advice that turns out to have been used to further a criminal purpose, though you were not aware of this at the time, so the privileged circumstances defence does not apply. At paragraph 5.7.2 of the Law Society's Practice Note on anti-money laundering, the Law Society cites the Crown Prosecution Service's guidance for prosecutors to state that if a solicitor forms a genuine, privileged circumstances (which is the case here), and the crime/fraud exemption does not apply, then the solicitor will be prevented from making a disclosure. However, you have inadvertently given advice that turns out to have been used to further a criminal purpose, though you were not aware of this at the time, so the privileged circumstances defence does not apply. At paragraph 5.7.2 of the Law Society's Practice Note on anti-money laundering, the Law Society cites the Crown Prosecution Service's guidance for prosecutors to state that if a solicitor forms a genuine, but mistaken, belief that the privileged circumstances exemption applies, the solicitor will be able to rely on the reasonable excuse defence.

stem: You have been instructed by a new client in respect of an advice on a matter of copyright law.
ask: The client is very informal and relaxed about the retainer and doesn't see the need for a written contract with you - the advice will be relatively straightforward and the extent of the instructions, the fixed fee and the fee earners who will work on the matter were made quite clear to and agreed by the client in the Do you need a written contract with the client?

options.en: A written contract is not legally necessary, but is strongly recommended to ensure that you act in the client's best interests, comply with the SRA Code of Conduct and that the extent and nature of the retainer is clear
A written contract is not legally necessary, but is strongly recommended to • ensure that you act in the client's best interest. You are free to agree whatever terms you wish with the client
A written contract evidencing the retainer is mandatory, and you cannot act under any circumstances without one

A written contract evidencing the retainer is mandatory, but you can act for the client until a written contract is drafted and signed between you and the client where the matter is urgent or the delay would otherwise prevent the client's instructions from being carried out
A written contract is not mandatory, but it is a legal requirement the oral agreement is evidenced, such as by an attendance note

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is A. A written contract is not legally necessary, but is strongly recommended to ensure that you act in the client's best interests, comply with the SRA Code of Conduct and that the extent and nature of the retainer is clear. As a solicitor, you must treat your client fairly (01.1) and provide services to your client in a manner which protects their interests in their matter, subject to the proper administration of justice. Clearly, the best way of fulfilling these outcomes is to ensure that there is a contract between you and your client which sets out each side's terms, conditions and obligations to one Conduct and that the extent and nature of the retainer is clear. As a solicitor, you must treat your client fairly (01.1) and provide services to your client in a manner which protects their interests in their matter, subject to the proper administration of justice. Clearly, the best way of fulfilling these outcomes is to ensure that there is a contract between you and your client which sets out each side's terms, conditions and obligations to one another, and that both the contract and its contents comply with the SRA Code of Conduct. While a written retainer is advisable (IB1.1, 1.3 and 1.19), it is not legally necessary.

stem: One of Parliament's main roles is debating and passing laws. Draft bills are issued for consultation before being formally introduced to Parliament. This allows proposed changes to be made before the bill's formal introduction.
ask: When a bill passes through the Houses of Parliament, which 'stage' follows the Second Reading of a bill?

options.en: When a bill passes through the Houses of Parliament the stage that follows the Second Reading of a bill is known as the Third Reading
When a bill passes through the Houses of Parliament the stage that follows the Second Reading of a bill is known as the Committee Stage
When a bill passes through the Houses of Parliament the stage that follows the Second Reading of a bill is known as the Report Stage
When a bill passes through the Houses of Parliament the stage that follows the Second Reading of a bill is known as the Royal Assent
When a bill passes through the Houses of Parliament the stage that follows the Second Reading of a bill is known as the Third Stage

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. When a bill passes through the Houses of Parliament the stage that follows the Second Reading of a bill is known as the Committee Stage. The Committee Stage can last for one or two days to eight or more. It usually starts no fewer than two weeks after the Second Reading. The day before the Committee Stage starts, amendments are published in a Marshalled List - in which all the amendments are placed in order. Amendments on related subjects are grouped together and a list ("groupings of amendments") is published on the day. Every clause of the bill has to be agreed to and votes on the amendments can take place. All proposed amendments ("proposals for change") can be discussed starts no fewer than two weeks after the Second Reading. The day before the Committee Stage starts, amendments are published in a Marshalled List - in which all the amendments are placed in order. Amendments on related subjects are grouped together and a list ("groupings of amendments") is published on the day. Every clause of the bill has to be agreed to and votes on the amendments can take place. All proposed amendments ("proposals for change") can be discussed and there is no time limit - or guillotine - on discussion of amendments. If the bill has been amended it is reprinted with all the agreed amendments. At the end of committee stage, the bill moves to report stage for further examination.

stem: A local authority invited tenders to operate a concession to supply school meals to all its local schools. It sent invitations to the existing operator and five other potential operators. A tender was submitted by a company, which was unsuccessful, even though it had submitted the highest tender.
ask: Which of the following statements best explains the legal position?

options.en: In this particular context, a tender is a contractually binding document
In this particular context, a tender is a contractually binding document when it is an offer made to an individual, group or the whole world and the company
In this particular context, a tender is not an offer to grant a concession to the person making the highest tender, but merely an invitation to treat
In this particular context, a tender is an offer to grant a concession to the person making the highest tender, not merely an invitation to treat
In this particular context, while a tender request will amount simply to an invitation to treat, the person making it is obliged to accept the highest tender

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. The invitation to tender in the scenario is no more than a proclamation of willingness to receive offers. The local authority is not bound to accept the highest or any tender. An invitation to tender in this form is an invitation to treat, and no contract of any kind can come into existence unless or until, if at all, the local authority chooses to accept any tender or other offer. Lead case: Spencer v Harding (1870) LR 5 CP 561.

stem: A married woman with two children, who has also been financially supporting her mother, dies in a fatal accident which has been caused due to the negligence of another person. The woman's husband was unemployed for several months at the time of her death. The woman also had a younger sister with physical disability whose house she cleaned every two weeks, and an old uncle for whom she had been cooking dinners once a week. The woman had been providing this support for her sister and uncle for several years until she died. Assume the dependants claim in the name of the executor or administrator of the deceased's estate.
ask: Under these circumstances, which of the following options best describes the full list of people within the woman's family who are entitled to claim damages against the wrongdoer, under the Fatal Accidents Act 1976?

options.en: The husband, children and the woman's mother
The children and the woman's mother
The husband, children, woman's mother and sister
The children, woman's mother and sister
The husband, children, woman's mother, sister and uncle

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The best answer is E. The husband, children, woman's mother, sister and uncle. Under the Fatal Accidents Act 1976, the following are eligible to claim in the name of the executor or administrator of the deceased's estate (known as 'dependants"): - a spouse or former spouse of the deceased, or person who was living as the spouse of the deceased, in the same household immediately before the date of the death and had been so living for at least two years; - any parent or other ascendant of the deceased or person treated by the deceased as his parent; - any child or other descendant of the deceased or any person who has been treated as a child of the family in • - in relation to any marriage of the deceased; - any person who is, or is the issue of, a brother, sister, uncle or aunt of the deceased. The fact pattern therefore suggests that the husband, children, woman's mother, sister and uncle are all 'dependants' as per the Fatal Accidents Act 1976. The woman provided financial support to her children, husband (who was unemployed for a long period before her death) and to her mother, as well as physical support to her disabled sister (cleaning) and old uncle (cooking). The heads of damage that can be - any person who is, or is the issue of, a brother, sister, uncle or aunt of the deceased. The fact pattern therefore suggests that the husband, children, woman's mother, sister and uncle are all 'dependants' as per the Fatal Accidents Act 1976. The woman provided financial support to her children, husband (who was unemployed for a long period before her death) and to her mother, as well as physical support to her disabled sister (cleaning) and old uncle (cooking). The heads of damage that can be claimed under the Fatal Accidents Act 1976 are dependency for both financial support and services. Hence, E is the best option.

stem: The European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention) is an international instrument, the correct interpretation of which can be authoritatively expounded only by the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR). explanation.en: nights Act 1998 C is correct. Domestic courts are required by section 2 (1) of the HRA to take into account any relevant Strasbourg case law. While such case law is not strictly binding, it has been held that courts should, in the absence of some special circumstances, follow any clear and constant jurisprudence of the Strasbourg court. stem: A man is a non-executive director of Example plc. The company's articles of association prohibit non-executive directors from entering into any contract on the company's behalf and provide that any contracts over £1,000,000 in value must be approved by the members of the company by way of ordinary resolution. Pursuant to a resolution of the board, the man contracts on behalf of the company in relation to a service provided by a woman, worth £5,000,000. The woman has obtained a copy of the company's articles and is aware of the restrictions on the power of the board and the man to enter into the contract.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes?

options.en: The woman cannot enforce the contract against the company, because the articles prohibit contracts of this nature
The woman cannot enforce the contract against the company, because the articles prohibit this and she was aware of this
The woman can enforce the contract against the company, because this was authorised by a board resolution
The woman can enforce the contract against the company, as it has been executed by a director
The woman can only enforce the contract against the company if it is subsequently ratified by ordinary resolution of the members

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. Section 40 of the Companies Act 2006 provides that a person dealing with the company is entitled to assume that directors have full power to bind the company, even if they are aware of a limitation on the powers of the directors. The woman will therefore be able to enforce the contract against Example plc without further ratification being necessary by the board or the members of the company.

stem: You are instructed to advise the trustees of a trust for three beneficiaries aged 26, 25 and 17 respectively. The trust asset is significant (real property) and is to be held on trust for the beneficiaries until they have all turned 25. However, the beneficiaries have communicated to the trustee that they all feel that their interests are best served by winding up the trust now and taking legal title to the property. The trust instrument is silent on the matter. Which of the following correctly advises the trustees? nave communicated to the trustee that they all teel that their interests are best served by winding up the trust now and taking legal title to the property. The trust instrument is silent on the matter.
ask: Which of the following correctly advises the trustees?

options.en: The trustees have no legal ability to wind up the trust and transfer legal title of the trust property to the beneficiaries
The trustees are compelled, if requested by the beneficiaries, to transfer legal title of the property to them
Despite the trust instrument remaining silent on variation, the trustees have a general discretion to modify the terms of the trust as they see fit, so can accede to the beneficiaries' wishes
The court may, on behalf of all the beneficiaries, vary the terms of the trust to fulfill the beneficiaries' wishes
The court may vary the terms of the trust to fulfill the beneficiaries' wishes, but cannot act on behalf of the beneficiary who is aged 17, as he is a minor

explanation.en: The best answer is D. The court may, on behalf of all the beneficiaries, vary the terms of the trust to fulfill the beneficiaries' wishes. A trustee can deviate from the terms of the trust with the consent of all of the beneficiaries, who must all be able to give consent. The two beneficiaries over the age of 18 can consent to the variation of the trust. However the beneficiary who is 17 cannot give their consent to the variation of the trust as they are a minor. The court has a power under section 1 of the Variation of Trusts Act 1958 to consent to a variation of a trust on behalf of a minor, but only where the variation would be for the benefit of that person.

stem: A long leaseholder of a penthouse apartment has leased the property to a woman by way of a two year parol lease. The woman is moving away from the area and agrees orally with the leaseholder that she will surrender the lease back to him. The leaseholder is happy to agree this, as he now thinks that he will get a higher rent for the property. After the woman has left, the leaseholder is unable to re-let the property and tells the woman that she owes him rent for the period that the property is unoccupied until he finds a new tenant. Throughout the course of the tenancy, the woman had been carrying on a business in the flat in breach of the terms of her lease. Which of the following statements would be correct as regards the surrender? leasenolder is nappy to agree this, as ne now thinks that ne will get a higher rent tor the property. After the woman has left, the leaseholder is unable to re-let the property and tells the woman that she owes him rent for the period that the property is unoccupied until he finds a new tenant. Throughout the course of the tenancy, the woman had been carrying on a business in the flat in breach of the terms of her lease.
ask: Which of the following statements would be correct as regards the surrender?

options.en: A surrender of the lease would have taken place at law and the woman would not be liable for rent due after the surrender
A surrender of the lease would have taken place at law but the woman would still be liable for rent due after the surrender
A surrender of the lease would not have taken place at law but the woman would not be liable for the rent
A surrender of the lease would not have taken place at law and the woman would still be liable for the rent
It is not possible to surrender a parol lease

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. A surrender of the lease would not have taken place at law and the woman would still be liable for the rent. Whilst the woman would be able to claim that an equitable surrender had taken place notwithstanding the lack of a formal Deed of Surrender, it would be unlikely that the court would allow the woman to enforce this equitable right against the leaseholder, because she herself has breached the terms of her lease. The equitable remedy of specific performance would therefore not be available to her, because she would not "come to equity with clean hands"

stem: A woman agreed to lure another woman to her boyfriend's flat, who she knew would be waiting with two other friends in order to have sex with the other woman. After plying the other woman with vodka and telling her they were going clubbing, the first woman actually took her to the three men, who were waiting at her boyfriend's flat. The other woman was then forced to have sex with all three men, whilst the first woman locked the door from the inside.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the woman's criminal liability, if?

options.en: The woman is guilty of conspiracy to rape and aiding and abetting rape
The woman is guilty of attempted rape, conspiracy to rape and aiding and abetting rape
The woman is guilty of rape, conspiracy to rape and aiding and abetting rape
The woman is guilty of conspiracy to rape and attempting to aid and abet rape
The woman is guilty of attempted conspiracy to rape and aiding and abetting rape

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. The woman is guilty of conspiracy to rape and aiding and abetting rape. A man or woman assisting a man to commit a rape can be prosecuted for the crime as an accessory. A woman can aid and abet a rape so as herself to be guilty of rape, and a boy at an age where he is presumed impotent can nevertheless aid and abet a rape. Similarly, a woman can be convicted of conspiracy to rape where she has participated in the plotting of the offence.

stem: The Scottish Nationalist Party (SNP) has agreed on a date for another referendum on Scottish independence. The SNP is considering what should be done, if anything, with the Crown Estates, should the Scottish electorate vote in favour of independence.
ask: You are asked to advise the SNP as to the current ownership status of the Crown Which option best advises the SNP?

options.en: The Crown Estate is owned by the Monarch 'in right of the Crown'
The Crown Estate is owned by the Monarch 'in rem of the Crown'
The Crown Estate is owned by the Monarch 'in personam of the Crown'
The Crown Estate is owned by the Monarch 'in respect of the Crown'
The Crown Estate is owned by the Monarch 'in flagrante delicto of the Crown'

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is the best option. The Crown Estate belongs to the reigning Monarch 'in right of The Crown', that is, it is owned by the Monarch for the duration of their reign, by virtue of their accession to the throne. But it is not the private property of the Monarch - it cannot be sold by the Monarch, nor do revenues from it belong to the Monarch. The Crown Estate is the property equivalent of the Crown jewels - part of the national heritage and held by Her Majesty The Queen as Sovereign, but not available for her private use.

stem: Your office pays £7,500.00 per month for its client management software.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: Credit software costs ledger Debit cash sheet office account (£7,500.00)
Debit general client ledger Debit cash sheet office account (£7,500.00)
Debit software costs ledger Credit cash sheet client account (£7,500.00)
No entries are required, because it is not in relation to a client matter
Debit software costs ledger Credit cash sheet office account (£7,500.00)

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is E. This is office money under Rule 12(7)(a), as it is money held in connection with running the practice (paying overheads). Client money is not involved. The office's costs ledger will record payments as they fall due and are paid. A payment is recorded as a debit, because it is an expense, and the payment from the office section of the cash account is recorded as a credit. A is wrong, because it records a receipt of monies into the cash account (rather than a payment) and an expense incurred (as opposed to discharged) on the software costs ledger. In essence, the CR and DR are the wrong way around. B is wrong, because this is an office expense, payable with office money, and is not in relation to a client matter. B is also wrong as there are two Debit entries which could not be correct. C is wrong, because it pays for the rental costs using client money, a clear breach of Rules 1(2), 13 and 14. D is wrong. Rule 29 does not require accounting records to be kept in relation to office money used for office matters only. However, Rule 1(2)(e) requires that establishes and maintains proper accounting systems, and proper internal controls over those systems, to ensure compliance with the rules. Since the money is drawn from the cash account, which may sometimes pay out monies on behalf of a client, or may sometimes have client money paid in (such as for professional disbursements incurred but not yet paid), it is necessary to ensure this transaction is recorded in order to comply with the Rules generally, and in particular Rule 1(2)(f), which requires proper accounting records to be kept to show accurately the position with regard to the money held for each client and trust.

stem: A catering company agreed to supply catering services to another company ("the buyer") for the entire busy summer season. As the summer progressed, the catering company found it increasingly difficult to cope because, they claimed, they had not set an adequate price for the work. The catering company negotiated a new deal with the buyer that an additional sum was to be paid after 10 further events, but when the 10th event was complete, the buyer refused to pay.
ask: Which of the following statements best advises whether there was any consideration for the promise to make the additional payments?

options.en: completion of the work

There was no consideration for the promise to make the additional payments, because there was an element of duress brought upon the buyer to pay the additional sum for what amounted to the catering company's performance of existing contractual obligations

There was no consideration for the promise to make the additional payments, because the catering company was only doing something they were already bound to do under the existing contract, so the promise by the buyer to pay the additional sum was gratuitous

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. The most appropriate defence available to the man under these circumstances is diminished responsibility. Diminished responsibility reduces the defendant's responsibility for the killing, and is seen as a partial defence in a case where, by definition, the defendant's level of culpability is established by reference to the traditional concepts of conduct and mens rea. Section 52 of the Coroners and Justice Act 2009 Act concerns the partial defence to murder of diminished responsibility as it applies in England and Wales. There is no change to the effect of successfully pleading the partial defence; it will continue to result in a verdict of manslaughter rather than murder (section 2(3) of the 1957 Act). stem: A charity operates to help homeless people. The charity exercises statutory functions which are of a public nature, although it is a private charity. Which statement best describes the charity's obligations under Human Rights Act which are or a public nature, although it is a private charity.

stem: A man and his friend are setting up a company. The man wants to set up a private limited company as he believes they will be able to start trading more quickly. The company can start trading once it has applied for a certificate of incorporation regardless of whether it is a public or private limited company

stem: In his will, a man leaves an annual sum of money to be used to pay for the recital of a religious mass in his memory on the anniversary of his death each year by the rector of his local church. ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

The man has created a charitable purpose trust that is not valid

stem: A man and woman own 123 The Street as joint tenants. stem: After World War II, former colonies and dominions became independent of Britain, bringing the British Empire to an end. George VI and his successor, Elizabeth II, adopted the title Head of the Commonwealth as a symbol of the free association of the independent countries comprising the Commonwealth of Nations. At present, 15 other independent Commonwealth countries share with the United Kingdom the same person as their Monarch.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the political structure of the United?

options.en: The United Kingdom is a federal state
The United Kingdom is a confederal state
The United Kingdom is an inter-governmental state
The United Kingdom is an absolute monarchical state
The United Kingdom is a unitary state

explanation.en: E is correct. The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland comprises four distinct countries: England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. Nevertheless, it is a unitary state. In a unitary system the central government commonly delegates authority to subnational units and channels policy decisions down to them for implementation. A majority of nation-states are unitary systems. They vary greatly. Great Britain, for example, decentralises power in practice though not in constitutional principle. Others grant varying degrees of autonomy to subnational units.

stem: X stated that: 'Y's article in the daily newspaper was incompatible with Y's advocacy of human rights'. Y has commenced defamation proceedings against X. X intends to plead truth and honest opinion. Assume that X's statement is defamatory.

stem: A man was gifted property in the form of a field some time ago. He decides to sell part of the field to a nearby farmer for £20,000. stem: A man and woman (not married) own 123 The Street (an unregistered property) together, having contributed equally to the purchase price. explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. The woman's interest will bind the buyer as it is an overriding interest. The interest of a person in actual occupation of the land will bind the buyer because it overrides a first registration, even if the occupier's interest was not obvious on a reasonably careful inspection of the land. Notice of either the occupation or the interest is unnecessary and the failure to protect a charge by entry or restriction on the Register of Title will not prejudice the person entitled, so long as the person is in actual occupation of the property. Hence, B is incorrect. Options C, D and E are all incorrect and refer to third party rights on unregistered land. If the couple were married the... - occupation or the interest is unnecessary and the failure to protect a charge by entry or restriction on the Register of Title will not prejudice the person entitled, so long as the person is in actual occupation of the property. Hence, B is incorrect. Options C, D and E are all incorrect and refer to third party rights on unregistered land. If the couple were married the woman would also have the benefit of Matrimonial Home Rights which could be registered as a Class F Land Charge, and this would be in addition to her equitable interest in the property deriving from her contribution to the purchase price. An equitable interest would neither appear on the title deeds nor be registered with its own title number.

options.en: Damages are appropriate if the consequence was within the parties' contemplation, and that consequence was a serious possibility, even if the consequence could not have been foreseen
Damages are awarded to compensate the applicant rather than punish the defendant

Lead case: Kingsley v United Kingdom (2002). 35 EHRR 177. Statute; rule; constitution: S. 8(3) HRA 1998.

stem: After learning of plans to build a new toxic waste landfill site in their town, the residents of a city decided to hold a public meeting. stem: The claimant contracted dermatitis because, he asserts, there were no washing facilities at his place of work. The defendant employer argues that there are multiple potential tortfeasors who all contributed to the risk that the claimant might contract Which of the following statements best describes how the courts evaluate the burden of proof needed to demonstrate causation, in particular, if there are multiple causes potential tortteasors who all contributed to the risk that the claimant might contract Which of the following statements best describes how the courts evaluate the burden of proof needed to demonstrate causation, in particular, if there
ask: are multiple causes?

stem: A prisoner was kicked and stamped to death whilst being detained on remand by his cell-mate, a dangerous and mentally ill man. Information had been available to show that the cell-mate was a real and serious risk to others. The prisoner's family now wishes to take proceedings against the prison authorities.
ask: Taking in to account European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) jurisprudence, who would have the burden of proof in such proceedings?

options.en: Neither party bears the burden of proof, because the ECtHR conducts a purely inquisitorial enquiry, not an adversary proceeding
The burden of proof is on the victim's cell-mate
The burden of proof is on the victim's family
The burden of proof is on the prison authorities
The burden of proof rests equally between the victim's family and the prison authorities

explanation.en: D is correct. The burden of proof is on the authorities to provide a 'satisfactory and convincing explanation' or a 'plausible explanation' for the events leading to a detainee's death. Lead case: Velikova v Bulgaria, No. 41488/98, 18.5.00, paragraph 70. Statute; rule; constitution: Article 2 ECHR.

stem: A man supplied cutting equipment to another person, not knowing whether the equipment would be used to commit a crime. The other person used the cutting equipment to commit a burglary.

stem: A settlor executes a trust in which she appoints her accountant to act as one of the trustees. The two remaining trustees are English solicitors based in London. The accountant is based in Jersey where she spends much of her time administering trust funds for large corporate clients.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes?

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. The appointment of a trustee who is not resident in the UK is not itself valid and would not invalidate the trust. stem: A person has owned a third of a share in a partnership for 15 years. There are two other partners. The person wants to know if the value of his share will be liable for Inheritance Tax (IHT) when he dies.

Business relief for the replacement asset in that case is generally •г - that the person owned the partnership share for at least two years prior to death, 100% business relief is available, meaning that Inheritance Tax will not be paid on the partnership share. stem: A man and woman discuss setting up a partnership and make certain agreements regarding the business. explanation.en: The correct answer is E. There are no registration requirements and a partnership agreement does not need to be in writing. Providing a partnership is intended by the parties, then the partnerships exists by virtue of the persons carrying on a business in common with a view to profit. The SRA takes no notice of trial outcomes and relies on the outcomes of its own investigations
The trial outcome will carry significant weight, but ultimately the SRA will still • conduct a separate and independent investigation and reach its own conclusion, separate to the trial outcome
The former employee must launch a separate complaint to the SRA - the trial outcome is self-contained
The trial outcome gives rise to automatic sanctions against the firm and its managers under the SRA Code of Conduct

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is A. The SRA will likely regard the firm has having breached its obligations in respect of equality and diversity by virtue of the trial outcome per se. The standard set by the SRA is very high. Being subject to any decision of a court or tribunal of the UK, that you have committed, or are to be treated as having committed, an unlawful act of discrimination is, per se, likely to amount to a breach of professional conduct (IB2.4). However, the Code does not go so far as to yield automatic sanctions following a finding of unlawful discrimination against a firm by a UK court or tribunal.

stem: A (fictional) United Kingdom law prohibits the importation and export of gold coins minted before 1947. A person imports a quantity of antique gold coins that were no longer legal tender.
ask: He also imports a quantity of sovereigns that are still legal tender Which of the following statements best describes whether the coins are 'goods' for the purposes of EU law?

options.en: The antique gold coins are 'goods' for the purposes of EU law, but the sovereigns are not
The sovereigns are 'goods' for the purposes of EU law, but the antique gold oins are no
Neither the antique gold coins nor the sovereigns are 'goods' for the purposes of EU law
Both the antique gold coins and the sovereigns are 'goods' for the purposes of EU law

The antique gold coins are 'goods' for the purposes of EU law, but the sovereigns constitute the "provision of a service", within the meaning of the Treaty provisions relating to the freedom to provide services

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. The free movement of goods provisions does not apply to coins that are legal tender and thus a means of payment. However, since the antique gold coins were no longer legal tender, they are, accordingly, goods. Lead case: Case 7/78, Rv. Thompson.

stem: You act for a volume claimant personal injury firm which also offers residential conveyancing. An accident management company has referred you the claim - arising in England - of a man who lives in a remote part of Scotland. You obtain his written consent to proceed but are unlikely to meet him in person during the course of the litigation.
ask: Which of the following best describes how you should proceed with respect to customer due diligence?

options.en: You must undertake enhanced customer due diligence
You must undertake standard customer due diligence
You must undertake simplified client due diligence
You cannot act for this client unless and until you meet them in person
You can act for this client but must meet them in person during the course of the transaction

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. Regulation 14(2) of the Money Laundering Regulations 2007 requires that where the customer has not been physically present for identification purposes, specific and adequate measures to compensate for the higher risk must be taken. This can include using additional documents, data or information to verify the customer's identity, or using electronic verification in addition to standard verification measures. You should, therefore, undertake enhanced customer due diligence if you wish to act for this client.

stem: A claimant became ill after eating liver pâté that had negligently been contaminated with salmonella. She wishes to bring an action in damages and asks you what she might expect, if her claim is successful.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the general principle which lies behind the award of damages in a tort action?

options.en: The general principle which lies behind the award of damages in a tort action is to restore the benefit conferred to the non-breaching party
The general principle which lies behind the award of damages in a tort action is for liquidated damages
The general principle which lies behind the award of damages in a tort action is to punish the defendant
The general principle which lies behind the award of damages in a tort action is to financially compensate the claimant
The general principle which lies behind the award of damages in a tort action is to restore the claimant to their original position

explanation.en: E is correct. The general principle which lies behind the award of damages in a tort action is to restore the claimant to the position which they were in before the tort was committed, as far as this can be done by an award of damages (where the claimant has lost a limb, for example, no amount of money can adequately compensate them for his loss or injury).

stem: A solicitor accepted £25,000 from a client. Rather than transferring the money into the business account, however, he transferred it into his personal account.
ask: Which of the following best states the solicitor's criminal liability, if any, under the Fraud Act 2006 (the Act)?

The solicitor may be charged with fraud by failing to disclose information under the Act
The solicitor may be charged with fraud by abuse of position under the Act
The solicitor is not criminally liable under the Act, because financial gain extends only to property, not cash
The solicitor is not criminally liable, under the Act, since there is no evidence that he intended to make a financial gain

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. By transferring the money into his personal account, he abuses his position as solicitor and acts against the financial interests of his client. Statute; rule; constitution: S. 4 Fraud Act 2006.

stem: A freehold owner of 123 The Street, which is an unregistered leasehold property in a compulsory registration area, grants a first legal mortgage to a bank.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The grant of the mortgage will trigger compulsory first registration of the estate
The grant of the mortgage will trigger compulsory first registration of the estate only if there are 21 or more years left to run on the lease
The grant of the mortgage will trigger compulsory first registration of the estate only if there are more than seven years left to run on the lease
The grant of the mortgage will trigger compulsory first registration of the estate only if there are three or more years left to run on the lease
The grant of the mortgage will not trigger compulsory first registration of the estate

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. The grant of a mortgage over an unregistered leasehold estate with more than seven years left to run will trigger compulsory first registration of that estate. This mirrors the provisions for first registration on the grant of a lease, with a lease granted for more than seven years being compulsorily registrable in order to take effect at law.

stem: A famous model was receiving treatment from a rehabilitation clinic. The details of the treatment and the visual portrayal of her leaving a specific meeting with other addicts were reported in a national newspaper. The model is seeking advice regarding the newspaper's disclosure.
ask: Which right or rights, if any, are engaged under the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention)?

options.en: The scenario engages the model's right to protection from discrimination
The Convention is not engaged, because the facts in the scenario merely disclose an equitable claim for breach of confidence
The scenario engages the model's right to a private life
The Convention is not engaged, because the Human Rights Act 1998 (HRA) does • not have horizontal effect, i.e. it does not apply to actions between private individuals
The Convention is not engaged, because a right of privacy is not recognised in English law

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. The model's right to a private life is engaged in the scenario. The HRA gives effect to the right to privacy (guaranteed by Art 8 of the ECHR). Lead case: Campbell v. MGN Ltd [2002]. Statute; rule; constitution: Article 8 ECHR.

stem: A complainant seeks to challenge the actions of a European Union (EU) institution, which it claims is acting beyond its powers. The complainant argues that the EU institution has a lack of competence, namely that it has acted in an area where it does not have the power to do so.
ask: Which option best states the method by which the legality of the act of the EU institution is being challenged?

options.en: A reference for a preliminary ruling
An action for failure to fulfil an obligation
An action for annulment
An action for failure to act
An action for damages

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is the best option. The European Court of Justice gives rulings on of cases are: references for a preliminary ruling; actions for failure to fulfil an obligation; actions for annulment; actions for failure to act; and actions for damages. The scenario discloses an action for annulment. The purpose of actions for annulment (Article 263 TFEU) is to have binding legal instruments (other than recommendations and opinions) of the Council, Commission, European Parliament or European Central Bank annulled. Statute; Rule; Constitution: Article 263 TFEU

stem: A Member of Parliament (MP) for a certain constituency is speaking at a meeting of his constituents in support of a new toxic waste landfill site, which has been earmarked for their area. He asserts that the proposed site will bring jobs to the area. A person sitting in the public gallery stands up, walks toward the MP and attempts to hit him in the face with a paper plate filled with shaving foam, before being brought Which is the most likely offence, if any, that may have been committed under the Public Order Act 1986 (the Act)? earmarked tor their area. He asserts that the proposed site will bring jobs to the area.
ask: A person sitting in the public gallery stands up, walks toward the MP and attempts to hit him in the face with a paper plate filled with shaving foam, before being brought Which is the most likely offence, if any, that may have been committed under the Public Order Act 1986 (the Act)?

options.en: The most likely outcome is that no offence has been committed in relation to the Act
The man's action under the circumstances constitutes an offence of violent disorder
The man's action under the circumstances constitutes an offence of affray
The man's action under the circumstances constitutes an offence of causing fear or provocation of violence
The man's action under the circumstances constitutes an offence of causing harassment, alarm or distress to another person

explanation.en: E is correct. Given the circumstances, a charge of behaviour causing harassment, alarm or distress in a public place under Section 5 of the Act is appropriate (nobody hurt, no apparent intent on serious violence, one person acting alone etc....) stem: A Member of Parliament (MP) has been charged with offences relating to claims for parliamentary expenses under the Theft Act 1968. The MP is seeking legal advice as to whether the criminal courts are prevented from trying him as an MP on charges relating to expenses claims, on the basis that the proceedings would infringe parliamentary privilege.
ask: Which of the following statements represents the most appropriate advice to give to?

options.en: The crown court has no jurisdiction to try the MP in respect of these charges, as • this would infringe parliamentary privilege, because the Bill of Rights 1689 protects MPs' right of free speech in Parliament

The crown court has jurisdiction to try the MP in respect of these charges, as neither the Article 9 of the Bill of Rights 1689 nor the exclusive jurisdiction of Parliament poses a bar to the jurisdiction of the crown court to try the MP in these circumstances
The crown court has no jurisdiction to try the MP in respect of these charges, as this would infringe parliamentary privilege, because of the exclusive jurisdiction (or cognisance) of Parliament
The crown court has jurisdiction to try the MP in respect of these charges; while honest claims are covered by parliamentary privilege, dishonest ones are not

The crown court has no jurisdiction to try the MP in respect of these charges, because the Bill of Rights 1689 protects MPs' rights of free speech in Parliament and because of the exclusive jurisdiction (or cognisance) of Parliament

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. Neither Article 9 of the Bill of Rights 1689, nor the exclusive jurisdiction/cognisance of the House of Commons poses any bar to the jurisdiction of the crown court to try the MP in these circumstances. The Supreme Court ruled in Rv Chaytor and others [2010] UKSC 52 that Parliamentary Privilege could not be used as a defence to claims of false accounting against Members of Parliament concerning their expenses. Lead case: Rv Chaytor and others (Appellants) [2010] UKSC 52. Statute; rule; constitution: Article 9 Bill of Rights 1689.

With regards to the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957 (the Act), which of the following statements best describes the parties' liability, if any, for the postman's electrocution? in to luxury tiats. Ine architect contracted an electrician to do the rewiring. Ine postman entered the property in order to deliver a letter, but when he rang the doorbell he was electrocuted, due to faulty installation work by the electrician.
ask: With regards to the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957 (the Act), which of the following statements best describes the parties' liability, if any, for the postman's electrocution?

options.en: According to the Act, the property owner would not be liable, because the damage was caused by the negligence of an independent contractor
According to the Act, the property owner would be liable, because he does not appear to have been reasonable in employing the architect
According to the Act, the property owner would be liable for not making sure that the architect was sufficiently competent

explanation.en: ..". You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. The occupier will not normally be liable for damage caused by the negligence of persons who were carrying out work on his premises, such as independent contractors. stem: A government minister is charged with responsibility for the execution of a bill's progress through Parliament. He is unsure what requirements are placed on him by the Human Rights Act 1998 (the Act) and the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention), and is seeking advice about how to proceed.
ask: Which of the following best states how the minister should proceed?

options.en: The minister must make a written statement that he considers the bill to be • compatible with the Convention rights, or that he is unable to make such a statement, but the government wishes to proceed with the bill anyway

The minister may make a written statement that he considers the bill to be • compatible with the Convention rights, or that he is unable to make such a statement, but the minister wishes to proceed with the bill anyway

The minister must make a verbal statement that he considers the bill to be compatible with the Convention rights, or that he is unable to make such a statement, but wishes Parliament to proceed with the bill anyway

The minister may make a verbal statement that he considers the bill to be compatible with the Convention rights, or that he is unable to make such a statement, but wishes Parliament to proceed with the bill anyway

The minister must make a statement, with the approval of the Prime Minister, that he considers the bill is compatible with the Convention rights, or that he is unable to make such a statement, but wishes Parliament to proceed with the bill anyway

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is the best answer. Under Section 19 of the Act, a minister must make a written statement that in his view the provisions of the bill are compatible with the Convention rights, or make a statement to the effect that, although he is unable to make a statement of compatibility, the government nevertheless wishes to proceed with the bill.

stem: A man and woman want to set up a company in order to regulate the local charitable organisation they run. Although they don't have any capital in order to form the company, members of the charitable organisation pay a monthly membership fee. The man thinks they can set up a company limited by guarantee, but the woman thinks the only option available is to set up an unlimited company.
ask: Which of the following best describes the current legal position?

options.en: A company limited by guarantee can only operate with over 100 members
A company limited by guarantee must be a public limited company
A company limited by guarantee only limits the liability of members, not directors
A company limited by guarantee does not require a share capital to start trading
A company limited by guarantee must have a share capital of at least £10,000 to start trading

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. A company limited by guarantee is generally formed for the purposes of clubs of charitable organisations. It does not require a share capital and generally raises funds from membership fees.

stem: A trustee authorises a transfer of £100,000 of trust money into his current account. The account already contains £100,000 of his own money and he uses the £200,000 to purchase two small properties in a town for £100,000 each, which he rents out to tenants. He saves the rental income in a separate savings account.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The trust funds could be traced into the current account, followed into the properties and followed into the savings account
The trust funds could be followed into the current account, traced into the properties and traced into the savings account
The trust funds could be traced into the current account, traced into the properties and traced into the savings account
The trust funds could be followed into the current account, followed into the properties and followed into the savings account
The trust funds could be traced into the current account, followed into the properties and traced into the savings account

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. Following can occur where legal title to the trust property has not passed and it has not been mixed with any other property. This would not be the case where trust money has been paid into a bank account containing other money. On the other hand, tracing can occur where legal title to the asset has passed or it has been mixed with other homogenous property and is no longer readily identifiable. The funds would, therefore, be traced to the current account, traced into the properties (as they were given in exchange for the trust money) and could also be traced into the rental income in the savings account as an unlawful profit.

stem: Your client is engaged in an argument with his landlord about repair of a chimney stack in the client's home, rented from the landlord. Your client installed the fireplace system and chimney himself. The landlord argues that the chimney stack is a fitting, since it is attached to the building and not the land and can be removed without demolishing the building; therefore it is not covered by the landlord's repair obligations in the lease, which cover only fixtures. Your client argues that it is a fixture, because it is attached to the house and is an essential part of the fireplace Which of the following is the correct answer? demolishing the bullding; theretore it is not covered by the landiord's repair obligations in the lease, which cover only fixtures.
ask: Your client argues that it is a fixture, because it is attached to the house and is an essential part of the fireplace Which of the following is the correct answer?

options.en: The chimney stack is a fixture; even though it is annexed to the building, it is so annexed for more convenient use of the building itself
The chimney stack is a fitting; even though it is annexed to the building, it is so annexed for more convenient use of the chimney in its own right
The chimney stack is a fitting; it is not sufficiently annexed to the building to be a fixture
The chimney stack is a fitting; fixtures can only be annexed to land, not buildings
The chimney stack is a fixture; its annexation to the building is prima facie evidence of its nature

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. The chimney stack is a fixture; even though it is annexed to the building, it is so annexed for more convenient use of the building itself. Per the House of Lords case of Elitestone Limited v Morris [1997] 1 WLR 68, the question of whether an object is a fixture or fitting turns on the facts, but that it depends on the degree of annexation to the land and the object (or purpose) behind the annexation. Whilst the degree of annexation will usually be one of common sense (such as a free-standing object that is not inseparably part of a building being considered a fitting), the purpose behind the annexation relates to whether the object has been fixed for more convenient use as a • - 1---- part of a building being considered a fitting), the purpose behind the annexation relates to whether the object has been fixed for more convenient use as a fitting or more convenient use of the land or building. In this question, it is clear that a chimney which forms part of a fireplace system is suitably annexed to the building and thus essential for use of the fireplace system, and thus the building, even though the chimney stack itself can be removed without demolishing the building. It will, therefore, be considered a fixture. Further, the case of Hulme v Brigham [1943] KB 152 confirmed that chimneys will be considered fixtures.

stem: The owner sold a disused 19th century building to a buyer. Both parties believed that the building was ripe for renovation. After completion of the contract, the building was listed by English Heritage as a building of historic and architectural interest. This has rendered the anticipated renovation virtually impossible.
ask: Which of the following statements best advises the parties of their respective rights under these circumstances?

options.en: The contract is void, because an operative mistake will render a contract void
The contract is void, because there is a mistake as to possibility of performing the contract
The contract is void, because there is a mutual mistake whereby both parties contracted, but contemplated different facts
The contract is not void, because there is no mistake as to the existence of the subject matter of the contract (res extincta)
The contract is not void, because there was no mistake when the parties entered in to the contract

explanation.en: E is the best option. The contract is not void; there was no mistake when the parties entered in to the contract. Mistake occurs where either one or both of the purportedly contracting parties believe that one set of facts exist, and this belief is subsequently shown to be wrong. This will render a contract void. The mistake must, however, precede completion of the actual contract. Since no mistake existed when the parties entered in to the actual agreement, the contract cannot be void, because the mistaken belief that the building was not designated of historic or architectural interest was not operating to induce the buyer to enter in to the contract; the mistake must have induced the mistaken party to enter in to the contract. F purportedly contracting parties believe that one set of facts exist, and this belief is subsequently shown to be wrong. This will render a contract void. The mistake must, however, precede completion of the actual contract. Since no mistake existed when the parties entered in to the actual agreement, the contract cannot be void, because the mistaken belief that the building was not designated of historic or architectural interest was not operating to induce the buyer to enter in to the contract; the mistake must have induced the mistaken party to enter in to the contract. Lead case: Amalgamated Investment and Property Co Ltd v John Walker & Sons [1976].

stem: A case concerning the death of a young offender, while he was being detained in a young offender's institute, is being heard by an inquest jury. A government minister wishes to raise critical questions in the House of Commons on the policies in force at that institution.
ask: The minister's questions relate to questions being considered by the Which option best expresses the rule or constitutional convention which is employed in these circumstances?

options.en: The constitutional convention that ministers must appear before Parliament directs that government ministers are required to make policy or ministerial announcements before Parliament, thus ensuring openness and transparency of the workings of their department of or in government
The constitutional convention of collective ministerial responsibility directs that • government ministers are expected to support government policy in Parliament and in public
The constitutional convention of individual ministerial responsibility directs that • government ministers are responsible to Parliament for their decisions and for the conduct of their departments
The constitutional convention of parliamentary privilege means that whatever is • said in debate in either chamber of Parliament is protected from prosecution by the courts
The sub judice rule directs that ministers should not mention in debates, questions, and motions cases which are pending or being heard by the court

explanation.en: E is the best option. Under the unwritten British constitution, there are two important conventions that help to preserve judicial independence. The first is that Parliament does not bring up in debates, questions, and motions cases which are pending or being heard by the court. The second is the principle of parliamentary privilege: that Members of Parliament are protected from prosecution in certain circumstances by the courts. The first of these above- mentioned conventions is known as the sub judice rule. The rule is justified on two separate grounds: (1) decisions of the courts should not be fettered or prejudiced by advance publicity, and should only be decided on the evidence presented in those courts; and by the court. The second is the principle of parliamentary privilege: that Members of Parliament are protected from prosecution in certain circumstances by the courts. The first of these above- mentioned conventions is known as the sub judice rule. The rule is justified on two separate grounds: (1) decisions of the courts should not be fettered or prejudiced by advance publicity, and should only be decided on the evidence presented in those courts; and (2) Parliament and the courts should not trespass upon each other's jurisdiction, and that debates in Parliament should not presume to come to a decision on a matter for which the courts are responsible. This is sometimes referred to as the principle of "comity". - J

stem: A judge rejected counsel's argument that the binding effect of an EU Treaty in domestic law did not depend solely upon the terms of its incorporation by the European Communities Act 1972, but also upon the higher principle of the supremacy of EU law, independent of national law. The judge stated, however, that while he had to reject the argument, perhaps it was time for courts in the UK to recognise such a hierarchy.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes which legal doctrine the judge's remark falls under?

The statement falls under the legal doctrine of the stare decisis
The statement falls under the legal doctrine of per incuriam
The statement falls under the legal doctrine of ejusdem generis
The statement falls under the legal doctrine of obiter dictum

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. E is correct. The statement falls under the legal doctrine of obiter dictum; comments by a judge that appears in a court's opinion, but do not form part of the court's decision.

stem: A man set an unoccupied warehouse on fire and is subsequently arrested. You are called to the police station to advise him prior to police interview. The man explains that he was acting according to instructions by local gangsters, who told him that they would expose the fact that he was gay if he didn't do it.
ask: Which of the following best states the man's defence, if any, to any criminal liability arising from his actions?

options.en: The man would not have a defence under these circumstances, because duress is not a defence to a charge of arson
The man would not have a defence under these circumstances, because a threat • to expose his homosexuality would not be sufficient to overbear the will of an ordinary person
The man would probably have a defence based on self-defence

In the case of Valderrama-Vega, R v [1985] CA, the defendant imported drugs. Colombian drug dealers had threatened to kill or injure him and his family if he did not comply. He was also under financial pressure and had been threatened with disclosure of his homosexuality. It was held that the threat to expose the defendant to criminal charges was not itself a defence (though it could be considered in mitigation of sentence), but that so long as the threats of physical violence were sine qua non to the defendant's decision, the other factors too could be --------3 mitigation of sentence), but that so long as the threats of physical violence were sine qua non to the defendant's decision, the other factors too could be taken into account. Similarly in R v Singh 1973, the Court of Appeal held that a threat to expose the defendant's adultery would not be sufficient threat to overbear the will of an ordinary person. For these purposes, the defendant must have a reasonable and genuinely held fear of death or serious harm, usually in the form of specific threats directed at the defendant, his immediate family or someone for whom he feels responsible. The director has no actual authority - i.e. that which is express (where an agent is expressly told he may act on behalf of a principal) or implied (authority by virtue of being necessary to carry out an agent's express authority, by the director acting as de facto managing director, or by acquiescence by the board to the conduct over a period of time).
