Per the Freeman case, the following criteria are met in this case: (1) that a representation that the agent had authority to enter on behalf of the company into a contract of the kind sought to be enforced was made to the contractor; (2) that such representation was made by a person or nersons who had "artual" authoritv to manane the the kind sought to be enforced was made to the contractor; (2) that such representation was made by a person or persons who had "actual" authority to manage the business of the company either generally or in respect of those matters to which the contract relates; (3) that he (the contractor) was induced by such representation to enter into the contract, that is, that he in fact relied upon it; and (4) that under its memorandum or articles of association the company was not deprived of the capacity either to enter into a contract of the kind sought to be enforced or to delegate authority to enter into a contract of that kind to the agent.

stem: The trustees of a large charitable trust based in a town wish to purchase a building to be used by the trust as office space for itself. explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Section 8 of the Trustee Act 2000 gives trustees an unrestricted power to acquire freehold or leasehold land as an investment, for occupation by the beneficiary or for any other reason.

stem: A company objected that it was not liable to pay a government agency liquidated damages for delay to completion of contract works. The company asserted that the damages were a disguised penalty.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the meaning of liquidated?

Liquidated damages are intended to punish the defendant for their behaviour

Liquidated damages mean an amount determined by the court

explanation.en: D is correct. The parties to the contract may make a genuine pre-estimate of damage in advance of any breach of contract of those losses which are likely to result in the event of a breach - and stipulate that such sum shall be payable in the event of a breach of contract.

stem: A man persuaded his wife to help kill his business partner. The wife agreed to lure the partner to some woods, where the man would be waiting to attack him; however, the wife's car broke down on the day of the plot, so the plan was abandoned. Both the man and his wife have been charged with conspiracy to commit murder.
ask: Which option best advises the parties?

options.en: The man may be charged with conspiracy to commit murder
The wife may be charged with conspiracy to commit murder
The man and his wife may be charged with conspiracy to commit murder
Neither the man nor his wife may be charged with conspiracy to commit murder
The man and his wife should not be charged with an offence because there was no actus reus present (i.e. causation)

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is the best answer. Neither the man nor his wife is guilty of conspiracy, since it is a purely spousal agreement. Section 2(2)(a) of the Criminal Law Act 1977 provides that a person is not guilty of a statutory conspiracy: "...if the only other person... with whom he agrees [is] (both initially and at all times during the currency of the agreement)... his spouse or civil partner..." Since no third-party is involved neither are criminally liable.

stem: Partners in a firm have all invested capital equally and expected to remove funds from the firm equally. However, one of the partners claims that she puts more work in and should, therefore, be entitled to receive a larger share of the capital. The two other partners disagree.

stem: A company owns a freehold plot of land. It constructs a block of flats and grants long leases of the flats to residents. The company transfers the block of flats to another company, retaining the surrounding land. The selling company omits to include part of the access road onto the public highway (which crosses the land that it has retained), meaning that the residents of the block must cross the selling company's land with vehicles for access. Which of the following statements best describes the position immediately after the transfer to the buying company? land with venices tor access. options.en: The buying company and the residents of the block can no longer gain access to the block of flats
The buying company and the residents of the block have an implied easement of necessity over the selling company's land
The buying company and the residents of the block have an intended easement over selling company's land

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. An easement of necessity would not be implied, as pedestrian access can still be gained directly from the highway. As the access road was meant to be included in the transfer, no intended easement over the land could exist. Section 62 of the LPA1925 would not operate to imply easements into the transfer as the plot of land and block of flats were in common ownership at the time of the transfer to the selling company. However, the criteria for the rule in Wheeldon v Burrows would be met, as the quasi- easement of way was apparent, in use at the time of the sale (by the tenants of the block) and necessary for the reasonable enjoyment of the land.

stem: A retiring partner believes that once retired, he will have no liability for the debts incurred whilst he was working for the partnership.
ask: Advise the partner of the current legal position regarding this area of law?

options.en: Retiring partners have no liability for debts incurred during their time at the firm
Retiring partners have partial liability for debts incurred during their time at the firm

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. Retiring partners remain liable for debts incurred whilst they were at the firm, per Section 17 Partnership Act 1890, unless the retiring partner is discharged from any existing liabilities by an agreement to that effect between himself and the members of the firm and the creditors. This agreement may be either expressed or inferred as a fact from the course of dealing between the creditors and the firm as newly constituted.

stem: A woman is the proprietor of 123 The Street, which she holds on a long lease with 860 years left to run. The woman has granted a charge by way of legal mortgage over the leasehold estate to a bank. She wishes to grant a sublease for two years over the property.

stem: A man went in to a supermarket and saw a flat screen TV on a shelf with a sign saying "Special Offer only £9.99". He took the TV from the shelf, put it in his trolley, and went to the checkout counter. He was told that the sign is wrong and should read £99.99.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the type of contract, if any, that has been formed?

options.en: It is generally accepted that the display of goods within a shop is an offer and not an invitation to treat
It is generally accepted that the display of goods within a shop is an invitation to treat and not an offer
An offer made to an individual, group or the whole world binds the offeror
Provided the advertisement is not mere 'puff' then the advertisement will be deemed sufficiently clear to constitute an offer
The type of contract that has been formed is a unilateral contract

explanation.en: B is correct. It is generally accepted that the display of goods within a shop is an invitation to treat and not an offer. Lead case: Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain v Boots Cash Chemists (Southern) Ltd. [1953].

stem: The School Bus Act 2011 (fictitious) provides that each local council shall have the duty to subsidise school bus services within its area in the interests of school pupils. A district council decided to subsidise school bus services within its boundaries provided by a man, who is the brother of the local mayor.
ask: The local mayor publicly stepped aside from the decision making process, however, and did not participate at all in the decision by an independent committee of the council to award the subsidy to his Which is the best statement regarding the courts' attitude if such a scenario presents itself in judicial review proceedings?

options.en: The best ground for judicial review raised by the council's decision to subsidise school bus services provided by the man is the right to a fair hearing
The best ground for judicial review raised by the council's decision to subsidise school bus services provided by the man is the duty to give reasons
The best ground for judicial review raised by the council's decision to subsidise school bus services provided by the man is the duty to consult
The best ground for judicial review raised by the council's decision to subsidise school bus services provided by the man is that the decision was biased

explanation.en: E is correct. Although bias may be present, if it is not demonstrated that the interest has influenced the decision, and if the mayor can clearly show that he did not participate at all in the decision making process, it is possible that the decision might stand, despite the potential of bias.

stem: A company is seeking the annulment of the European Commission's ("the Commission") 'soft fruit' decision by making an application to the Registry of the General Court, in respect of bringing an action against the Commission.
ask: The company is concerned to bring the action within the time-limits laid down by the annulment Which option best advises the company as to the time-limits for such an application?

Statute; Rule; Constitution: Article 263(6) TFEU

stem: A man was injured in a road accident caused by another person's the defendant's negligence, necessitating the amputation of the man's right leg. Due to the operating surgeon's negligence, the man's left leg was amputated instead. The person who has caused the accident defendant asks you for advice. You are expected to explain what the term novus actus interveniens indicates.
ask: Which option best advises the defendant?

options.en: The term novus actus interveniens signifies directness of damage
The term novus actus interveniens signifies remoteness of damage
The term novus actus interveniens signifies foreseeability of damage
The term novus actus interveniens signifies directness and remoteness of damage
The term novus actus interveniens signifies directness, remoteness and foreseeability of damage

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. The term novus actus interveniens signifies remoteness of damage. When the court considers whether a novus actus interveniens has occurred, if the damage that resulted was the reasonably foreseeable result of the defendant's negligence (or if it did would be discounted by him as being so remote that no precautions were required), no event in the sequence of events was a novus actus interveniens. In other words, if it was reasonably foreseeable that D1s act would cause D2 to act negligently, then D1 is liable. Lead Case: Lamb v Camden London Borough Council [1981] 2 All ER 408.

stem: A local authority conducted itself in a manner which infringed the rights of a parent and child under the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention).
ask: The judge must now consider the proper relief, to grant the victims of the local authority's Which option best states the relief the judge may grant, if any, in the proceedings?

options.en: The court may grant such relief as it considers just and appropriate, provided it is within its powers
The court may grant such relief that it considers compatible with the Convention, provided it is within its powers
The court may grant such relief as it considers relevant, provided it is within its powers
The court may grant such relief that takes in to account the decisions of the European Court of Human Rights
The court may grant such relief as it considers fair and equitable, provided it is within its powers

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. Section 8(1) of the Human Rights Act 1998 (HRA) provides that, where a court holds that a public authority has or will be acting contrary to the HRA, then it may grant such remedy as it considers "just and appropriate". Normally, remedies are in the form of declarations, injunctions and prerogative orders. As we see from sections 4(6) read with 6(2)(a), remedies are limited in terms of the relief that they might offer. Sections 8(1-4) further restrict remedies.

stem: A shareholder in a private limited company wishes to see a copy of the company's annual reports. It has been five months since the end of the financial year and the shareholder thinks the company has violated her rights by not sending a copy.
ask: Which of the following best describes the legal position?

options.en: A shareholder has the right to see a copy of the company's annual report prior to the end of the financial year
A shareholder has the right to see a copy of the company's annual reports within one month of the end of the financial year
A shareholder has the right to see a copy of the company's annual reports within three months of the end of the financial year
A shareholder has the right to see a copy of the company's annual reports within six months of the end of the financial year
A shareholder has the right to see a copy of the company's annual reports within 12 months of the end of the financial year

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. Shareholders have a right to receive a copy of the annual accounts within six months of the end of the financial year of the company.

stem: A woman executes a will in which she leaves £100,000 on trust for the members of a local club (the Club), an unincorporated association. She specifies that the gift is to form part of the Club's funds and be administered in all respects in accordance with the rules for the time being of the Club. After the woman's death, her children challenge the gift to the Club. They argue that as the Club has no legal personality; it cannot enforce the terms of the trust against the beneficiaries and, therefore, the trust has failed.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The trust has failed for lack of certainty of objects
The trust operates as a gift to the individual members of the Club and therefore its objects are certain
The trust operates as a contract-holding gift and therefore its objects are certain
The trust operates as a gift to be held for the association as a quasi-corporate entity and therefore its objects are certain
Although the objects are certain, a trust in favour of an unincorporated association will always fail

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is C. The gift is treated as being held for the members for the time being of the club subject to their contractual rights and responsibilities towards each other in accordance with the rules of the Club. Rather than membership of the club simply being a means to identify a finite list of beneficiaries, the Club's members from time to time are classed as the beneficiaries at that point.

stem: Your clients are the shareholders of a private limited company. The company has recently been incorporated, and your clients need some direction as to the correct terms used by HMRC for Corporation Tax purposes.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes HMRC's position?

options.en: The tax accounting period can be longer than 12 months, in certain circumstances
The tax year matches the accounting year and runs for the 1st of April to the 31st of March each year
The tax year matches the accounting year and runs from the 6th of April to the 5th of March each year
The tax accounting period cannot be more than 12 months
Limited companies are required to submit annual accounts to Companies House, including a profit and loss account, which matches the tax accounting period as per HMRC

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is D. The accounts tax period cannot be more than 12 months. In such event, you must file two Company Tax Returns because you will have two Corporation Tax accounting periods. For example, if the company has its accounts prepared for 15 months from the 1st of January 2012 to the 31st of March 2013, your Corporation Tax accounting periods will be: • 1st of January 2012 to 31st of December 2012(12 months); • of of January to to of of March 2013(3 months). You will need to file two Company Tax Returns to cover these two Corporation Tax accounting periods. • 1st of January 2013 to 31st of March 2013(3 months). You will need to file two Company Tax Returns to cover these two Corporation Tax accounting periods. A is incorrect. Tax accounting period cannot be longer than 12 months. This is as opposed to an 'accounting period'. For instance, your accounts can cover a period of more than 12 months if your newly-formed company is preparing its first accounts to cover a period of more than 12 months, or your existing company changes its financial year end. B is incorrect. The tax year does not necessarily always matches the accounting year of a company. C is incorrect. The tax year does not necessarily always matches the accounting year of a company, and in any in any event does not run from the 6th of April to the 5th of March each year (which is the individual's tax year). E is incorrect. A Corporation Tax accounting period is different from similar terms used by other HMRC tax areas (such as VAT accounting periods) or other Government agencies (such as Companies House accounting reference periods). Limited companies are required to submit annual accounts to Companies House, including a profit and loss account, which does not necessarily matches the tax accounting period as per HMRC.

stem: A woman transfers part of her freehold land to a second woman. She includes in the transfer deed an obligation upon the second woman "and her successors in title not to use the land transferred for the purposes of carrying on the profession of a solicitor." The woman subsequently transfers the land that she has retained to a third woman. The second woman transfers her land to a man.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: The third woman would enforce the covenant against the first woman at common law
The third woman would enforce the covenant against the man at common law
The third woman would enforce the covenant against the first woman in equity
The third woman would enforce the covenant against the man in equity
The third woman can not enforce the covenant against the first woman or the

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. The benefit of the covenant has not passed to the third woman in accordance with common law rules, as the covenant does not touch and concern the retained land. It will therefore be necessary to establish whether the benefit has passed to her in equity. No words of annexation have been used and, as the covenant does not touch and concern the land, statutory annexation by virtue of s.78 Law of Property Act 1925 is not applicable. The third woman cannot, therefore, enforce the covenant against anyone.

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. The courts hold that if A appeared in person before B, impersonating C, an innocent purchaser from A gets the property in the goods against B. Lead case: Lewis v Averay [1971] 3 WLR 603, CA.

stem: Your firm is concerned at recent public criticism of firms that do not appear to have sufficient diversity within their workforces. explanation.en: ra Code of You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is C. The SRA Code of Conduct neither forbids nor mandates positive action. Individual solicitors and firms are not required to implement "positive discrimination" by promoting minority groups, but they are required to provide services to clients in a way that respects diversity (O2.2). stem: Your client wishes to proceed with a slip and fall claim against a local authority. You have established that this is a civil claim, but need to be sure of which first instance court, or courts, the claim form should be sent to.

stem: Historically, the medieval monarchy was both feudal lord and head of the kingdom. stem: You act for a public company - Alternative Investment Market (AIM) listed, on a corporate restructuring.
ask: Which of the following best describes how you should proceed with customer due diligence?

options.en: As this is a listed company trading on a regulated market, you may undertake simplified customer due diligence
As this is a listed company but trading on an unregulated market, you must apply standard customer due diligence
As this is a listed company but trading on an unregulated market, you may conduct either simplified or standard customer due diligence on a risk-based approach
As this is a listed company trading on a regulated market, you do not need to undertake any client due diligence
As this is a listed company but is trading on an unregulated market, you must undertake enhanced client due diligence

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. Under Regulation 13(3) of the Money Laundering Regulations 2007, where a customer is a company whose securities are listed on a regulated market subject to specified disclosure obligations, simplified due diligence applies. However, AIM is not a regulated market. Regulation 7(3) states that customer due diligence must be carried out on a risk-sensitive basis and be able to demonstrate to his supervisory authority that the extent of the measures is appropriate. Therefore, you may feel that the company's profile and self-regulation requirements required to list on AIM are sufficient to warrant simplified client due diligence.

stem: A woman gained entry to a free, but invite-only, musical event. In order to gain entry she represented herself as an invited guest.

The woman only obtains a service by a dishonest act if the services are made available on the basis that payment, has, is being or will be made for them, and she obtains these services without any payment or without full payment. Statute; rule; constitution: S. 11 Fraud Act 2006.

stem: You advise the members of a Limited Liability Partnership ("LLP") that provides legal services. Owing to increased and unsustainable competition in the legal services market and a desire for the members to pursue other interests, they are seeking to wind up the LLP. The LLP is solvent with sufficient assets to pay off its creditors in full.
ask: How can a solvent LLP bring its business activities to an end?

options.en: Members' voluntary liquidation
Creditors' voluntary liquidation
Compulsory liquidation
Voluntary strike-off and dissolution
Administrative Receivership

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is A. Members' voluntary liquidation. A members' voluntary liquidation is the process to follow when an LLP is solvent and has sufficient assets to be able to pay creditors in full, including costs. The process involves making - and filing with Companies House - a declaration of solvency. A liquidator is then appointed to take control of the LLP and its assets in order to sell the assets of the LLP and distribute any remaining money to creditors after paying costs and expenses of the liquidation. stem: A woman enters into an arrangement with man whereby the woman is entitled to occupy the top floor of the man's house (consisting of a bedroom and bathroom) in exchange for a fee of £50 per week. The man has granted the woman a personal license, which must be registered at HM Land Registry

The man has granted the woman a personal license, which cannot be registered at HM Land Registry

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. The nature of the agreement is such that the woman can not be said to have exclusive possession of the property; rather, her arrangement is more like that of a lodger who shares communal areas with her landlord. As she does not have exclusive possession of the whole of the property, the arrangement cannot be a lease and is a license. As a license is a personal contractual arrangement, it does not create an interest in land and can not be registered.

stem: A woman is the freehold owner of 123 The Street. She executes a declaration of trust in favour of her friend over the land.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the nature of the friend's interest in the land?

options.en: The friend has a legal interest in the land
The friend has an equitable interest in the land which is converted into a legal interest once it has been registered
The friend has a legal interest in the land which is converted into an equitable interest once it has been registered
The friend has an equitable interest in the land
The friend has an equitable interest in the land as long as it is registered

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. The interest of a beneficiary under a trust is an equitable interest in the land. There is no need for it to be registered in order for it to take effect.

stem: The ultra vires doctrine in judicial review proceedings means that, where an administrative authority exceeds its statutory power, the court can intervene. It is a fundamental constitutional principle, therefore, that all powers exercised by administrative authorities are conferred by Acts of Parliament. In light of the above, which of the following is an exception to the constitutional principle that all powers exercised by administrative authorities
ask: are conferred by Acts?

options.en: An exception to the constitutional principle that all powers exercised by administrative authorities are conferred by statute is the doctrine of locus standi
An exception to the constitutional principle that all powers exercised by administrative authorities are conferred by statute is the Human Rights Act 1998
An exception to the constitutional principle that all powers exercised by administrative authorities are conferred by statute is the exclusivity rule
An exception to the constitutional principle that all powers exercised by administrative authorities are conferred by statute is the proportionality principle
An exception to the constitutional principle that all powers exercised by administrative authorities are conferred by statute is the royal prerogative

explanation.en: E is correct. While the constitutional theory of judicial review has long been dominated by the doctrine of ultra vires, under which a decision of a public authority can only be set aside if it exceeds the powers granted to it by Parliament, the courts have also declared the decisions taken under the royal prerogative to be amenable to judicial review. Lead case: Council of Civil Service Unions v Minister for the Civil Service [1985] AC 374. Note: It is important to understand that while prerogative powers were originally exerted by the reigning Monarch, most of these residual powers are.. p. - -gative prerogative powers were originally exerted by the reigning Monarch, most of these residual powers are now exercised by Ministers of State independently from the Monarch or at least through the advice they provide to the Monarch which he/she is constitutionally bound to follow. These residual powers that are vested in the Executive may be challenged, but not the Monarch's personal prerogative powers. This means that modern day courts may scrutinise the manner in which such powers are exercised by judicial review, which allows such Ministerial acts to be challenged on grounds of illegality (ultra vires) and indeed unreasonableness, or procedural unfairness. - -gative

stem: Two people are in partnership in a law firm together. One is buying a house. The other is acting on the transaction. Shortly before completion, the buyer gives the acting principal an amount of money representing the balance of the purchase price.
ask: Which of the following best reflects the correct reasoning and best accounting entries to process the money?

explanation.en: The best answer is E. This is office money and should be paid into the office bank account and recorded in the office side of the buyer's ledger account. The only person entitled to the money until completion is the buyer, a principal in the firm. Under Rule 12.8, a principal in the firm cannot be their own client, so the money is office money. Having a ledger account does not mean that the buyer is a client of the firm - under Rule 29.11, you are required to provide bank statements in relation to any office account. Operating a ledger account for the buyer to account for the mortgage payment in the office allows you to keep an accurate record of payments made that are not in LIL VITILL MIVE YUU LU AULM UIE accurate record of payments made that are not in relation to a client or trust matter. Answer A is wrong because even though the partner is not a client of the firm, neither is the purchase money in relation to capital purchased by the firm, so this would be an incorrect record of the treatment of the office money. Answer B is wrong because there is no such thing as an office designated deposit account. Under Rule 12.8, a principal in the firm cannot be their own client, so the office is office money. Under Rule 13.5, a separate designated client account is an account relating to Answer B is wrong because there is no such thing as an office designated deposit account. Under Rule 12.8, a principal in the firm cannot be their own client, so the office is office money. Under Rule 13.5, a separate designated client account is an account relating to money for a single client. There is no such thing as a separate designated office account; there is simply the general office bank account. Answers C and D are wrong because this is office money, not client money. Under Rule 14.2, only client money may be paid into a client account. As this is office money, you would be breaching Rule 14.2 by paying it into a client account.

stem: The Governance of Britain Green Paper published in July 2007 included a number of proposals to reform the royal prerogative. The government intended both to pass powers from government to Parliament and make powers exercised under the prerogative subject to greater scrutiny by Parliament. Which of the following statements best describes the role of a Green Paper in proposals to retorm the royal prerogative. The government intended both to pass powers from government to Parliament and make powers exercised under the prerogative subject to greater scrutiny by Parliament.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the role of a Green Paper in?

options.en: The primary function of a Green Paper is a consultative government report of a proposal without any commitment to action
The primary function of a Green Paper is to set out the government's official statement of guidance and good practice
The primary function of a Green Paper is to set out the government's proposals for legislation on particular subjects
The primary function of a Green Paper is to enforce amendments to clauses in Parliamentary bills on particular issues
The primary function of a Green Paper is to set out the timetable for completion of different stages of a bill's progress through the House of Commons

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. The primary function of a Green Paper is a tentative consultative government report of a proposal without any commitment to action. Green papers typically set out the government proposals, their context, and initial responses to them. They also consider the mechanisms by which the Green Paper, dubbed as "the first step in a national conversation", will involve Parliament and the public in further reform.

stem: A man and his friend are also business partners. The friend is the freehold owner of a property at 123 The Street and executes a transfer of his legal and equitable title to the property in favour of the man for no consideration.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The man is the absolute owner of 123 The Street and does not hold the property on trust for the friend, because the presumption of advancement applies
The man holds the property on trust for the friend on an automatic resulting trust, as he did not make a declaration of trust
The man holds the property on trust for the friend on a presumed resulting trust, as the transfer was voluntary and at nil consideration
The man holds the property on trust for the friend on a presumed resulting trust, because the presumption of advancement does not apply
The man holds the property on trust for the friend on an automatic resulting trust, because of the failure of an express trust

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. The presumption of advancement would not apply and therefore since the transfer was made at nil consideration, a presumed resulting trust would arise in favour of the friend.

stem: Your client purchased a house from a man for its market value and complied with all legal formalities. Subsequent to the purchase, it transpires that the man was the trustee of a trust, and the house constituted trust property which was held for a beneficiary. Your client had no knowledge whatsoever of this state of affairs, and purchased the property genuinely believing it to be free of encumbrances; there was nothing in the Register of Title to indicate that the property formed part of the assets of a trust. The beneficiary is seeking to void the sale.
ask: Is your client's interest in the property protected?

options.en: No, because the beneficiary has a legal interest in the land that is enforceable against the world
No, because the beneficiary has an equitable interest in the land that is enforceable against the world
No, because your client had constructive notice of the beneficiary's interest, and he is therefore not protected by the doctrine of notice
Yes, because he is a bona fide purchaser for value without notice, and thus protected by the doctrine of notice
Yes, because he complied with all legal formalities and therefore his legal interest overrides the beneficiary's equitable interest

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. Yes, because he is a bona fide purchaser for value without notice, and thus protected by the doctrine of notice. In contrast to the degree of protection enjoyed by the holder of a legal interest, the holder of an equitable interest (i.e. beneficiaries under a trust) enjoys far less protection. Whereas legal interests "bind the world", whether an equitable interest binds third parties is determined by the doctrine of notice. The doctrine of notice states that "Equitable interests bind everyone except a bona fide purchaser for value without notice." A bona fide purchase for value without notice is one who, acting with clean hands, purchases the property for full --—- protection enjoyed by the holder of a legal interest, the holder of an equitable interest (i.e. beneficiaries under a trust) enjoys far less protection. Whereas legal interests "bind the world", whether an equitable interest binds third parties is determined by the doctrine of notice. The doctrine of notice states that "Equitable interests bind everyone except a bona fide purchaser for value without notice." A bona fide purchase for value without notice is one who, acting with clean hands, purchases the property for full consideration, with no actual knowledge of the beneficiary's interests and with no intention to deprive the beneficiary of that interest, which would be your client in this case.

stem: It has been a fundamental principle of the common law since its origins that justice is conducted, and judgments are given, in public. The principle of open justice must, however, yield to privacy or secrecy, but normally only when, in the circumstances of a particular case, to adhere to the principle of open justice would frustrate the court's ability to administer justice properly. Circumstances where open justice in civil proceedings can properly yield to privacy, therefore, are provided for by the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention) protection of open justice.
ask: Where a derogation from the principle of open justice is sought under the Convention, what must an applicant demonstrate?

options.en: It must be demonstrated that the derogation sought is strictly necessary to • enable the court to do justice, and is a proportionate means to facilitate the proper administration of justice
It must be demonstrated that the derogation sought is stringently sensible to • enable the court to do justice, and is a prudent means to facilitate the proper administration of justice
It must be demonstrated that the derogation sought is absolutely appropriate to enable the court to do justice, and is a practical means to facilitate the proper administration of justice
It must be demonstrated that the derogation sought is absolutely applicable to enable the court to do justice, and is a sensible means to facilitate the proper administration of justice
It must be demonstrated that the derogation sought is strictly serviceable to enable the court to do justice, and is a preferable means to facilitate the proper administration of justice

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. Derogations from the principle of open justice (enshrined in Article 6 of the Convention) can only be made where they are strictly necessary to enable the court to do justice, and are a proportionate means to facilitate the proper administration of justice. Lead case: Ntuli v Donald [2010] EWCA Civ 1276. Statute; rule; constitution: Article 6 European Convention on Human Rights.

stem: Fundamentally, burglary involves entering a building with a view to committing theft. It should be noted that whether or not there has been an entry will be a matter of fact, to be determined by the jury.

To prove the actus reus of the offence of burglary, the prosecution must prove • that the defendant entered a building or part of a building with a view to committing theft
To prove the actus reus of the offence of burglary, the prosecution must prove TAL

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. There are three elements to the actus reus of burglary which must be proved: That: (1) The defendant enters (2) A building or part of a building (3) As a trespasser. Statute; rule; constitution: 59 Theft Act 1968.

stem: A woman contracts with a man in return for the man's promise to decorate the woman's friend's house. The man reneges on the agreement.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the most appropriate outcome under the common law doctrine of privity of contract?

options.en: The friend can sue the man, and recover substantial damages for her own loss
The woman can sue the man, but can only recover nominal damages for her own loss
The friend can sue the woman and recover damages for her own loss
The woman can sue the friend and recover substantial damages for her own loss
The woman can sue the man on the friend's behalf for the loss sustained by the friend

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. Where a the contracting party (the woman) has made a contract with the man for her friend's benefit, the woman can sue the man, but can only recover nominal damages, since she suffered no financial detriment. The friend has no claim against the man; the loss is sustained by a third party to the agreement (the friend). Lead case: Woodar v Wimpey [1980] 1 WLR 277.

stem: The claimant lived opposite an oil depot. She suffered damage to her car caused by soot from the chimneys and damage to her clothes on the washing line.
ask: Which of the following statements best explains the difference between public nuisance and private nuisance?

options.en: interferes with the use or enjoyment of land or rights over land

A public nuisance deals with situations where a number of people are affected by the nuisance and it is not confined to interference with enjoyment of the property, whereas a private nuisance is any activity or state or affairs that interferes with the use or enjoyment of land or rights over land

stem: A man and his friend are discussing whether to set up a public or private limited company. The man thinks the issued share capital of a public limited company must be at least £100,000 whilst the friend believes it must be £50,000 with at least half paid up.
ask: Which of the following best describes the current legal position relating to public limited companies?

options.en: The issued share capital must be at least £100,000
The issued share capital must be at least £100,000 with a quarter paid up
The issued share capital must be at least £50,000 with a quarter paid up
The issued share capital must be at least £50,000 with half paid up
The issued share capital must be at least £25,000 with a quarter paid up

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. Public limited companies are required to have an issued share capital of at least £50,000 with at least a quarter paid up. This is intended to ensure that public limited companies have enough capital when they are formed and will not be wound up quickly.

stem: A claimant is aggrieved by a decision of an inferior tribunal and is considering of making an application to the Administrative Court by using the Civil Procedure Rules (CPR). The claimant's application may require the seeking of a prerogative order, or alternatively the claimant may seek a declaration or injunction. However, the claimant is unsure of the respective procedural requirements in regard to the Administrative Court's jurisdiction and judicial review. nich option best advises the claimant!
ask: Which option best advises the claimant?

options.en: The judicial review procedure must be used where the claimant is seeking a • prerogative order; it may be used where the claimant is seeking a declaration or injunction
The judicial review procedure must be used where the claimant is seeking a prerogative order; it must be used where the claimant is seeking a declaration or injunction
The judicial review procedure may be used where the claimant is seeking a • prerogative order; it may be used where the claimant is seeking a declaration or injunction
The judicial review procedure may be used where the claimant is seeking a • prerogative order; it must be used where the claimant is seeking a declaration or injunction
The judicial review procedure may neither be used where the claimant is seeking a prerogative order nor where the claimant is seeking a declaration or injunction

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is the best option. The judicial review procedure must be used where the claimant is seeking one of the so-called prerogative orders (or an injunction under s30 of the Senior Courts Act 1981 (SCA) to restrain person acting in office in which they are not entitled to act), namely, a mandatory order, prohibiting order or quashing order (formerly known as mandamus, prohibition and certiorari): CPR r.54.2. The judicial review procedure may be used where the claimant is seeking a declaration or injunction: CPR r.54.3 (1). See also SCA ss 31(1),(2). Applications for judicial review in the Administrative Court are governed by CPR Part 54 (previously RSC O.53). This is the judicial review declaration or injunction: CPR r.54.3 (1). See also SCA ss 31(1),(2). Applications for judicial review in the Administrative Court are governed by CPR Part 54 (previously RSC 0.53). This is the judicial review procedure referred to in section 31 of the SCA, to which reference should also be made (along with section 29, the High Court's jurisdiction to grant the prerogative orders). Note that it is also now possible in many cases for claims for judicial review to be transferred to, and sometimes to be commenced in, the Upper Tribunal: see Supreme Court Act 1981 s 31A. Statute; Rule; Constitution: CPR r.54.2; Supreme Court Act 1981 ss 31(1), (2).

stem: According to one theory, international law is regarded as automatically incorporated in municipal law. On the other hand, another theory indicates that international law is not ipso facto part of municipal law. A rule of international law will become part of municipal law only after the transformation of it into municipal law by means of regulation or through an Act of Parliament. Which of the following term stands for how international law is implemented pursuant to the dualist theory? • The dominant principle of the dualist theory is known as the Doctrine of is not ipso tacto part or municipal law. A rule or international law will become part or municipal law only after the transformation of it into municipal law by means of regulation or through an Act of Parliament.
ask: Which of the following term stands for how international law is implemented pursuant to the dualist theory?

options.en: The dominant principle of the dualist theory is known as the Doctrine of Incorporation
The dominant principle of the dualist theory is known as the Doctrine of Parliamentary Supremacy
The dominant principle of the dualist theory is known as the Doctrine of Positive Obligation
The dominant principle of the dualist theory is known as the Doctrine of Transformation
The dominant principle of the dualist theory is known as the Doctrine of Proportionality

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. The dominant principle of the dualist theory is known as the Doctrine of Transformation. The dualist theory treats international law and domestic law as separate. Its dominant principle is known as the Doctrine of Transformation. As per the Doctrine of Transformation, international law only forms a part of domestic law, if accepted as such by statute or by judicial decisions (or in the UK, under the royal prerogative). This doctrine has evolved from the ratification procedure.

stem: A man and his friend are in partnership together as stock brokers. They buy and sell shares on behalf of their clients as nominees, with all shares being held on trust for their clients in accordance with the terms of their retainer. They also buy shares on their own account. They are both made bankrupt and their trustees in bankruptcy try to claim that the shares held by the man and his friend on trust for their client form part of their bankruptcy estates.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the?

options.en: The two friends hold the shares for their clients on trust and therefore the shares do not form part of their bankruptcy estates
No trust exists over the shares held for their clients, as there is no certainty of intention and therefore the shares form part of their bankruptcy estates
No trust exists over the shares held for their clients, as there is no certainty of objects and therefore the shares form part of their bankruptcy estates
No trust exists over the shares held for their clients, as there is no certainty of subject matter and therefore the shares form part of their bankruptcy estates
No trust exists over the shares held for their clients, as there is no certainty of subject matter, objects or intention, and therefore the shares form part of their bankruptcy estates

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. The two friends hold the shares for their clients on trust and therefore the shares do not form part of their bankruptcy estates. Certainty of intention exists, due to the terms of the friends' retainer declaring that shares are held on trust for their clients. Certainty of objects exists, because the records of the friends' business will identify which shares belong to which client. There is certainty of subject matter, even if the shares are not individually identified, provided that they are of the same type and in the same company as any that the friends hold on their own account (Hunter v Moss [1994]).

ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: An easement of necessity would be implied into the transfer to the friend
An intended easement would be implied into the transfer to the friend
An easement would be implied into the transfer to the friend under the rule in Wheeldon v Burrows
An easement would be implied into the transfer to the friend by section 62 Law of Property Act 1925
The friend has no easement to draw water from the well

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. It would be difficult to establish necessity or an intention to make the grant, since it would be just as easy for the friend to have the cottage connected to the mains water supply. As the two tenements were in common ownership at the time of the grant, section 62 of the Law of Property Act 1925 would not apply. However the rule in Wheeldon v Burrows would apply to imply an easement into the transfer. This is because the right would be apparent, necessary for the reasonable enjoyment of the land and also in use at the time of the sale.

All Convention rights are regarded as equally important by the Convention. However, the degree to which the Convention right is open to derogation also changes from article to article.

The absolute rights contained in the Convention consist of: the right to life; the prohibition of torture; the right to a fair trial; and no punishment without law
The absolute rights contained in the Convention consist of: the right to life; the • prohibition of torture; the prohibition of slavery; and no punishment without law

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. Some human rights - like the right not to be tortured; the right to life; the prohibition of slavery; and no punishment without law - are absolute. stem: A client of a partnership is pleased with the work the firm has carried out for him and gives one of the partners a classic car as a gift. The partner who receives the gift is unsure whether he is able to keep it for himself or must the gift be made to the firm.

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. A partner cannot make unauthorised personal profit. stem: A director of a public limited company, a large multi-national conglomerate based in England, becomes aware that the company will shortly be announcing a large restructure which will most likely cause the value of its shares to increase. explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. stem: A husband was a partner in a partnership for 18 months and his interest in that partnership was worth £50,000. On the husband's death, the interest transferred to his wife. Six months later, the wife died, and the interest in the partnership transferred to her daughter.
ask: Does the interest attract business relief?

options.en: No, as an interest in a partnership does not constitute business property that may be eligible for the relief, under any circumstances
No, as the period of ownership ended when the interest transferred to the wife and was less than the two year minimum ownership period
Yes, as the ownership period is only six months
Yes, as business relief is available on the interest for the period in which the husband owned it, as well as the wife's period of ownership
No, as the period of ownership runs only from when the interest was transferred to the wife

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. Yes; business relief is available on the interest for the period in which the husband owned it, as well as the wife's period of ownership. An interest in a partnership that is owned by the transferor throughout the two years immediately before the transfer will be considered business property, for which 100% business property relief is available. However, if the transferor (i.e. the wife) became entitled to the property on the death of the transferor's spouse or civil partner, relief is available for any period during which the spouse or civil partner owned it. Thus, the ownership requirement ran from when the husband first acquired the interest, and in a partnership that is owned by the transferor throughout the two years immediately before the transfer will be considered business property, for which 100% business property relief is available. However, if the transferor (i.e. the wife) became entitled to the property on the death of the transferor's spouse or civil partner, relief is available for any period during which the spouse or civil partner owned it. Thus, the ownership requirement ran from when the husband first acquired the interest, and continued when the interest transferred to the wife. When the wife died and the interest transferred to her daughter, the combined total period of ownership is two years; thus, the interest attracts business relief.

stem: The trust deed of a private family settlement provides that its two trustees shall have a power to invest in land in order to generate income for the trust and increase the capital. stem: A woman placed an advertisement in her local newspaper offering a reward of £5,000 for information leading to the return of her pet dog. A man reads the advert. Later, when he sees a dog matching the description, he returns it to the woman.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the type of contract, if any, that has?

options.en: The type of contract that has been formed is a contract by deed
The type of contract that has been formed is a simple contract
The type of contract that has been formed is a bilateral contract
The type of contract that has been formed is a unilateral contract
No contract that has been formed, as the woman's offer was merely an invitation to treat

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. The type of contract that has been formed is a unilateral contract. A unilateral contract is one where only one party promises to do something in return for an act of the other party. In this case, the man is not obliged to find the dog, but on doing so, this becomes a condition precedent, and the woman is obliged to pay the reward. This contrasts with a bilateral contract, which would arise if the man promised to find the dog in return for the reward.

stem: A woman executes a declaration of trust in which she transfers a substantial portfolio of real estate into trust for the benefit of her granddaughter. She appoints the following people to act as her trustees: Pete (aged 26), Amy (aged 42), Erin (aged 17), Steve (aged 32) and Rachel (aged 56).

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. The man will pay CGT on the £50,000, minus the market value at the time he received the gift and minus any exemptions due. If the asset was a gift (rather than paid for) the capital gain is calculated using the market value at the time the asset was given. stem: Your client has the right to allow vehicles to traverse across an adjoining piece of land in order to access the back gate of his property. He isn't sure whether this right constitutes real or personal property.
ask: Does this right over land constitute real or personal property?

options.en: Real property, as it is an interest in the land, and real property can include a right in, over or derived from land
Personal property, as it is intangible

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. Real property, as it is an interest in the land, and real property can include a right in, over or derived from land. 'Real property' basically means an interest in land. Land is defined as "...land of any tenure, and mines and minerals, whether or not held apart from the surface, buildings or parts of buildings (whether the division is horizontal, vertical or made in any other way) and other corporal hereditaments; also a manor, an advowson, and a rent and other incorporeal hereditaments, and an easement, right, privilege, or benefit in, over, or derived from land...", per s205(1)(ix) of the Law of Property Act 1925. As can be seen, therefore, real property isn't always tangible - -3 tenure, and mines and minerals, whether or not held apart from the surface, buildings or parts of buildings (whether the division is horizontal, vertical or made in any other way) and other corporeal hereditaments; also a manor, an advowson, and a rent and other incorporeal hereditaments, and an easement, right, privilege, or benefit in, over, or derived from land...", per s205(1)(ix) of the Law of Property Act 1925. As can be seen, therefore, real property isn't always tangible property, and can include what are known as 'incorporeal hereditaments' - conceptual rights that exist 'only in contemplation' - in, over or derived from land, including rights such as those granted to your client. ask: The wording of a draft Bill states that its provisions govern future Acts and the provisions contained in the Bill cannot be subsequently amended or repealed by Considering the principle of Parliamentary sovereignty, are the provisions in the draft Bill likely to be binding if it becomes law?

options.en: No, because Parliament cannot bind itself in the future as to do so would be in breach of European Union law and Parliament's ability to comply with the same
Yes, because Parliamentary sovereignty is such that it can even bind itself in the future in such a way
No, because the provisions offend the sovereignty of Parliament and will be automatically unenforceable
No, because the courts will strike down the Act as offending the sovereignty of Parliament

No, because the courts will apply the principle of implied repeal such that the draft Bill, if it becomes law, will neither bind Parliament in the future nor prevent subsequent interference with or repeal of its provisions

explanation.en: The best answer is E. No, because the courts will apply the principle of implied repeal such that the draft Bill, if it becomes law, will neither bind Parliament in the future nor prevent subsequent interference with or repeal of its provisions. In addition to the restrictions on Parliament's power to make laws concerning anything - brought about by membership of the European Union - Parliament cannot pass a law that cannot be changed or reversed by a future Parliament. No Act of Parliament may be made secure from amendment or repeal by a future Parliament. In the event of a subsequent Act of Parliament that seeks to amend the offending Bill (then an Act) or that is inconsistent, the court will hold that the later Act takes precedence and the conflicting parts of the earlier Act are repealed. This is the principle of implied repeal. In Vauxhall Estates v Liverpool Corporation [1932] 1 KB 733, the court stated that, even if the Act could be construed as intending to govern future Acts which was doubtful, the relevant provisions must be regarded as being impliedly overridden by the inconsistent provisions of the later Act. In other words, no Act of Parliament can effectively provide that no future Parliament can interfere with its provisions.

The woman is approached by a gang of robbers who offer her £10,000 to make a copy of the keys so that they can steal goods from the shop. The woman agrees to assist the robbers, who subsequently take the money from the shop.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The £10,000 would be classified as an unauthorised profit by a fiduciary and the money would be held on resulting trust for the store owner
The £10,000 would be classified as an unauthorised profit by a fiduciary and would be held on constructive trust for the store owner
The £10,000 would be classified as the profit of an unlawful act by a fiduciary and would be held on resulting trust for the store owner
The £10,000 would be classed as the profit of an unlawful act by a fiduciary and would be held on constructive trust for the store owner
The £10,000 belongs to the woman

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. The £10,000 would be classed as the profit of an unlawful act by a fiduciary and would be held on constructive trust for the store owner. The woman has been involved in a robbery and therefore the court would impose a constructive trust upon the profits of such an act (see Brinks v Abu-Saleh (No 3) [1996]). The court would impose a fiduciary duty upon the woman by virtue of her position of trust and the proceeds of her breach would be held on constructive trust for her.

stem: 123 The Street is an unregistered freehold property. The legal title is vested in two men, who hold it on trust for themselves and for a woman, who occupies the property. The men grant a first legal mortgage to a bank to secure repayment of a loan. The bank's surveyor inspected the property prior to completion and was told by the woman that she has an interest in the property and occupies it. The grant of the mortgage does not trigger compulsory first registration of the estate.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The bank will be bound by the woman's interest, because it is an interest which overrides an unregistered disposition
The bank will be bound by the woman's interest, because it is an interest which overrides a registered disposition
The bank will be bound by the woman's interest, because it had notice of it
The bank will not be bound by the woman's interest, because it is a bona fide purchaser for value without notice
The bank will not be bound by the woman's interest, because her interest has been overreached

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. The bank will not be bound by the woman's interest, because her interest has been overreached. Because the property is unregistered and the transaction did not trigger compulsory first registration, the provisions of the Land Registration Act 2002 do not apply. The doctrine of notice would therefore be applied to establish the priority of the woman's equitable interest as against that of the bank, unless the woman's interest was overreached by the sale proceeds (i.e. the mortgage advance) being paid to at least two trustees. As the mortgage deed has been signed by both men, the woman's interest in the property is overreached and the bank takes its charge free from her interest.

stem: A creditor obtained judgment for a debt against debtor, who subsequently asked for time to pay. The creditor agreed that she would take no further action against the debtor, provided that he paid £500 immediately and the rest by half-yearly instalments of £150. While the debtor duly kept to his side of the agreement, judgment debts carry interest, and the creditor now claims the balance.
ask: Which of the following statements best advises the parties with regard to promissory?

options.en: The creditor will not be able to recover the balance of the interest, unless the creditor can show that some consideration was supplied in return for the creditor's agreement to take the lesser sum
The creditor will not be able to recover the balance of the interest if the payment of £500 on the due date is paid in good faith by the debtor
If the debtor provides goods, or services, instead of cash, this will discharge the • debt fully, because the gift of a 'horse, hawk or robe' may be more beneficial than the money
The creditor will still be able to recover the balance of the interest, unless the debtor can show that some consideration was supplied in return for the creditor's agreement to take the lesser sum
The debtor's promise was binding on her, because of sufficient consideration, and she cannot therefore, legitimately claim interest

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. The creditor will still be able to recover the balance of the interest, unless the debtor can show that some consideration was supplied in return for the creditor's agreement to take the lesser sum. The House of Lords held in Foakes v Beer (1884) that Mrs Beer was entitled to the £360 interest which had accrued. Foakes had not "bought" her promise to take no further action on the judgment. He had not provided any consideration. Lead case: Foakes v Beer (1884).

stem: Your accountant rings you to confirm whether separate client ledger accounts are required in your new matter, where you are acting for the borrower and an institutional lender in respect of a mortgage advance.
ask: Are separate client ledger accounts for the borrower and institutional lender?

options.en: No, provided both parties provide informed consent to the arrangement
No, provided that the funds belonging to each client are clearly identifiable and • the lender is an institutional lender which provides mortgages on standard terms in the normal course of activities
This is not permitted under any circumstances and is a clear breach of the provisions of the SRA Accounts Rules
No, provided that the funds belonging to each client are clearly identifiable and the lender is a private lender
No, provided that a designated deposit account is used for both parties

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. The funds belonging to each client are clearly identifiable and the lender is an institutional lender which provides mortgages on standard terms in the normal course of activities. This is Rule 29.10, the exception to Rule 29.2(b), which requires that all dealings with client money be on the client side of a separate client ledger account for each client. Where a private lender - as opposed to an institutional lender - grants a mortgage, two separate ledger accounts must be kept for both parties - the exception in Rule 29.10 is not available.

stem: A demonstration was called in response to the government announcing cuts in student funding. The demonstration turned violent when students broke in to, and occupied, a seven storey government building. An 18 year old student, who had climbed on the roof of the building along with at least 10 other demonstrators, dropped a fire extinguisher on to the street below, narrowly missing police officers.
ask: Which is the most likely offence, if any, that may have been committed in relation to the Public Order Act 1986 (the Act)?

options.en: The student's action under the circumstances constitutes an offence of riot
The student's action under the circumstances constitutes an offence of violent disorder
The student's action under the circumstances constitutes an offence of affray
The student's action under the circumstances constitutes an offence of causing fear or provocation of violence
The student's action under the circumstances constitutes an offence of causing harassment, alarm or distress to another person

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. Section 2 POA states: "Where three or more persons who are present together use or threaten unlawful violence and the conduct of them (taken together) is such as would cause a person of reasonable firmness present at the scene to fear for his personal safety, each of the persons using or threatening unlawful violence is guilty of violent disorder." Clearly a fire extinguisher dropped from the seventh floor constitutes violent disorder. Statute; rule; constitution: s. 2 Public Order Act 1986.

stem: Two men who want to set up a charity are unsure of the best type of business model but think they would like to form a partnership. Their friend warns them that a charitable venture would not satisfy the criteria of forming a partnership.
ask: Which of the following best describes the legal position?

options.en: A charitable organisation can be formed as a partnership
A charitable organisation cannot be formed as partnership
A charitable organisation can be formed as limited liability partnership
A charitable organisation can be formed when there are over five partners
A charitable organisation can be formed when there are over seven partners

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. A charitable organisation cannot be formed as partnership. The definition of a partnership is that it is the relation which subsists between persons carrying on a business in common with a "view of profit". A charitable organisation does not fulfil the 'business' criteria within this definition and cannot be carried out with a view to profit. Therefore, a charitable organisation cannot be set up as a partnership.

stem: A woman executes a will in which she leaves £10,000 to her friend "in the hope that she will use it in the manner that she knows I would have wished to have seen it used had I still been alive.

The transfer could not create a trust, because there is no certainty of objects or subject matter
The transfer could not create a trust, because there is no certainty of subject matter

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. The transfer could not create a trust, because there is no certainty of intention or objects. There is no certainty of intention, because it is not clear from the language used in the instrument that the woman intended to subject the property to a legally binding obligation for the benefit of persons or purposes. There is no certainty of objects, because it is not possible to identify from the instrument for whose benefit the trust property is to be applied.

stem: A woman has recently bought a child's car seat and some children's clothes. Examining her receipt, she sees she has been charged VAT at the standard rate. She complains to the shop and argues that she should not have been charged VAT at all.

The car seat is subject to VAT at the zero rate, but the clothes are subject to the standard rate
The clothes can be subject to the zero rate, whilst the car seat can be subject to the reduced rate

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Children's clothes can be subject to the zero rate of VAT, whilst the car seat can be subject to the reduced rate. However, the reduction in VAT rate will depend on the specific product and sale so the reduced rate cannot always be assumed.

stem: A woman executes a deed in which she grants her friend and her successors in title the right to pass drain water through a pipe which crosses the woman's land. The woman's land is registered. The right is granted for a fixed term of 100 years.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The woman has granted her friend a legal lease, which should be registered with its own title number and noted on the woman's title
The woman has entered into a positive covenant with her friend, which should be registered in the charges register of the woman's title
The woman has granted her friend an equitable easement, which should be registered in the charges register of the woman's title
The woman has granted her friend a legal easement, which should be registered in the charges register of the woman's title
The woman has granted her friend an equitable easement, which should be registered as a Land Charge

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. The woman has granted her friend a legal easement, which should be registered in the charges register of the woman's title. The woman has granted her friend an easement in the form of a right of way over her land. The easement operates at law, because it has been granted for a term of years absolute. In registered land, legal and equitable easements must be protected by way of notice on the charges register of the servient tenement in order to bind a purchaser of that land. They can also be registered in the property register of the dominant tenement.

The driver is liable for assault, because there was a continuing positive act, starting from when he moved the car to when he turned it off

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. stem: A woman applied for a mortgage, which was dependant on her earning more than £32,000 a year. She stated on the application form that she earned £35,000 a year. In fact, she earns less than £22,000 per year.

stem: A woman executes an inter vivos declaration of trust, by which she places a substantial sum of money on trust for an eight year old child. stem: A woman is the freehold owner of 123 The Street, a registered freehold property. She has split the property into flats and executed a lease over the ground floor flat in favour of her friend. The friend applies to register the lease at Land Registry and her application is cancelled, as the plans to the lease are defective.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The friend has no interest in the property
The friend is the proprietor of a legal term of years absolute and should protect this interest by entry of a notice on the woman's title
The friend is the proprietor of a legal term of years absolute and should protect this interest with a Restriction on the woman's title
The friend has the benefit of an estate contract and should protect this interest by entry of a notice on the woman's title
The friend has the benefit of an estate contract and should protect this interest with a Restriction on the woman's title

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. The friend has the benefit of an estate contract and should protect this interest by entry of a notice on the woman's title. The grant of a lease for more than seven years is a registrable disposition for the purposes of the Land Registration Act 2002. Therefore, until the lease is registered, the legal estate that it creates cannot pass to the lessee. Until the legal title has been perfected, the friend therefore has the benefit of a contract to grant the lease, which is a form of estate contract. Such an interest is protected by way of notice in the charges register of the burdened title.

stem: A man allegedly raped a mentally disabled woman. The law required the victim to make a complaint, but in this case the victim was unable to do so because of her mental disability. The State could not prosecute him.

stem: A woman agreed to buy 50 tons of fennel seed from a man. Statutory regulations provide that no person may buy fennel seed unless they have a licence from the Department of the Environment. The woman induced the man to sell her fennel seeds by fraudulently misrepresenting to him that she had a licence, and is now refusing to take delivery of the seed. nich ot the tollowing statements best advises the parties!
ask: Which of the following statements best advises the parties?

options.en: Contracts to commit a legal wrong or carry out conduct which is otherwise contrary to public policy are rendered unenforceable at common law, even if the innocent party is unaware that the intended act is contrary to the law or public policy

explanation.en: E is correct. An unmeritorious defendant, who is aware of and might even have induced the breach of statutory provision, may rely on a defence of illegality in order to defeat an honest claimant's claim. It is open to a party, however shabby it may appear to be, to say that the legislature has prohibited this contract and, therefore, it is a case in which the court will not lend its aid to the enforcement of the contract. In other words, contracts that are illegal by statute (or by public policy) are void and unenforceable at the time of formation - even if both parties are unaware of the facts causing the illegality and even if neither party had any intention of flouting the law. Re Mahmoud and Ispahani (1921) offers a helpful illustration of its aid to the enforcement of the contract. In other words, contracts that are illegal by statute (or by public policy) are void and unenforceable at the time of formation - even if both parties are unaware of the facts causing the illegality and even if neither party had any intention of flouting the law. Re Mahmoud and Ispahani (1921) offers a helpful illustration of statutory prohibition. When the parties transacted in linseed oil without the obligatory licences, the seller was unable to recover damages for the buyer's non- acceptance, even though the buyer had misrepresented that he possessed a licence. Lead case: Re Mahmoud and Ispahani [1921].

stem: A caretaker of a building lived with his wife in a house owned by the owners of the building. His wife was injured by a falling shelf, shaken out of place by vibrating machinery operating next door. She wishes to bring an action in nuisance against the machinery operators. Which of the following statements best describes who may bring an action in private macninery operators.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes who may bring an action in private?

options.en: The claimant in private nuisance may be a class of Her Majesty's subjects • whereby the nuisance materially affects their reasonable comfort and convenience of life
The claimant in private nuisance may be a class of Her Majesty's subjects living in the area whereby the nuisance materially affects their reasonable comfort and convenience of life
The claimant in private nuisance must normally be a person with a substantial link with the property affected
The claimant in private nuisance must normally be a person with a legal or equitable interest in the land affected by the nuisance
The claimant in private nuisance may be either a person with a legal or equitable interest in the land affected by the nuisance, or a relative or visitor

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. Normally, only those who have a legal interest in the land affected (i.e. a freehold or tenancy) can sue in private nuisance. A mere relative or visitor, however damaged or inconvenienced, has no cause of action. Lead case: Malone v Laskey [1907].
