stem: Three men are partners in a firm. Two of the partners decide to hire a fourth partner. The third partner is unhappy and argues that he had a right to decide on whether they should take on another partner.
ask: Which of the following best describes the legal?

options.en: If the majority of partners decide to take on another partner, then the decision stands
One partner can assert themselves to take on a senior partner role and make a decision of this nature
All partners must consent to the hiring of a new partner
Over 80% of the partners must consent to the hiring of a new partner
As long as more than 50% of the partners consent to the hiring of a new partner, then it is acceptable

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. All partners must consent to the hiring of a new partner. In the absence of suitable provision in a partnership agreement, Section 24(7) of the Partnership Act 1890 states that all existing partners must consent to the hiring of a new partner. However, a large partnership may wish to exclude the need for unanimity, e.g. to enable the senior partners to decide which partners should be promoted to senior partners and which to take on as junior partners - in which case they should make such provision in their partnership agreement.

stem: Your partner is acting for a client and is seeking an urgent interim injunction to prevent dissipation of trust property which would be untraceable.
ask: Which of the following represents the correct criteria that a court must consider before awarding an interim injunction?

options.en: That the balance of convenience indicates the grant of an award; that the applicant can demonstrate a good prima facie case; that there is a serious question to be resolved at trial; and that there is an undertaking for damages in the event that the applicant does not succeed at trial

That the balance of inconvenience indicates the refusal of an award; that the applicant can demonstrate a good prima facie case; that there is a serious question to be resolved at trial; and that there is an undertaking for damages in the event that the applicant does not succeed at trial

That it is necessary and that no common law remedy would be sufficient; the applicant must come to the court with clean hands; there must not have been delay on the applicant's part; and the respondent must not suffer undue harm as a result of the injunction

That the balance of convenience indicates the grant of an award; that the applicant can demonstrate a good prima facie case; that there is a serious question to be resolved by summary judgment after the awarding of an interim injunction; and that there is an undertaking for damages in the event that the applicant does not succeed at trial

That the balance of inconvenience indicates the refusal of an award; that the applicant can demonstrate a good prima facie case; that there is a serious • question to be resolved at trial; and that the applicant deposits sufficient funds with the court to cover damages and costs in the event that the applicant does not succeed at trial

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is A. That the balance of convenience indicates the grant of an award; that the applicant can demonstrate a good prima facie case; that there is a serious question to be resolved at trial; and that there is an undertaking for damages in the event that the applicant does not succeed at trial. This is the 'balance of convenience' test, set out in American Cyanamid v Ethicon Ltd [1975] AC 396 and are the factors the court must consider when considering whether to award an interim injunction. In essence, the court must consider, on balance and taking the factors into account, whether is it more convenient to grant or deny an injunction.

stem: A woman is the freehold owner of 123 The Street, a registered freehold property. In 2005, she grants a 10 year lease of the property to her friend. The lease contains a provision that allows the friend to renew the lease for a further period of five years at the end of the initial term. In 2007, the woman transfers the freehold to a man. The man refuses to allow the friend to exercise his right renew the lease as he didn't have actual knowledge of the friend's occupation before the disposition took place, and it was not obvious to him, on a reasonably careful inspection of the land, that the friend was occupying the property. Which of the following statements best describes the legal position? actual knowledge of the triend's occupation betore the disposition took place, and it was not obvious to him, on a reasonably careful inspection of the land, that the friend was occupying the property.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: The friend can enforce the covenant against the man by virtue of the doctrine of privity of estate
The friend can enforce the covenant against the man by virtue of the doctrine of privity of contract
The friend can only enforce the provision to renew the lease against the man if • the friend has registered it in the Charges Register as a notice on the freehold title

The friend cannot enforce the provision to renew the lease against the man, whether or not he has registered it in the Charges Register as a notice on the freehold title

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. The friend can only enforce the provision to renew the lease against the man if the friend has registered it in the Charges Register as a notice on the freehold title. A lease for more than seven years, which is granted out of a registered freehold, must be protected by registration of a notice in the Charges Register of the freehold title. According to Schedule 3 of the Land Registration Act 2002, a lease not protected in this manner will not bind a subsequent purchaser as an overriding interest, unless (i) it is obvious, on a reasonably careful inspection of the land, that the person claiming it is occupying the land (save if the person taking the disposition actually knows about the claimant's interest); (ii) an inquiry was made of the person claiming it, before the disposition took place and he failed to disclose it when he could reasonably have been expected to do so. As for option E, only the first part of the sentence is correct "The friend cannot enforce the provision to renew the lease against the man". So if the friend would not have registered the lease as a notice on the freehold title, the man's right would override the rights of the friend to renew the lease, as the man didn't have actual knowledge of the friend's occupation before the disposition took place, and it was not obvious to the man, on a reasonablv careful inspection of the land, r.- reasonably have been expected to do so. As for option E, only the first part of the sentence is correct "The friend cannot enforce the provision to renew the lease against the man". So if the friend would not have registered the lease as a notice on the freehold title, the man's right would override the rights of the friend to renew the lease, as the man didn't have actual knowledge of the friend's occupation before the disposition took place, and it was not obvious to the man, on a reasonably careful inspection of the land, that the friend was occupying the property. However the second part of option E is incorrect - "whether or not he registered the lease as a notice on the freehold title" - as registration would protect the friend's rights.

The partnership dissolved at the completion of the Olympics contract; therefore, neither partner is liable to the third party

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. The partnership continued as a partnership at will at the completion of the Olympics contract; therefore, both partners are liable to the third party. At the expiry of the fixed term of a partnership (in this case the duration of the Olympics contract) the partnership continues as a partnership at will on the same terms as the fixed partnership. This means that the partners continue to act as each other's agents and are able to bind each other into contracts. On that basis, both partners are liable to the third party for the performance of the contract.

stem: In her will, a woman leaves a sum of money to be used for the maintenance of her cat until he dies. She directs that the income is to be paid to her sister, who must use it to provide for the cat.

The trust should be contrasted with charitable trusts for the protection of animals or a class of animals in general. Trusts established for the maintenance of specific animals are held to be valid non-charitable purpose trusts.

stem: A young woman was raped and murdered by a gang of teenagers. The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) decided that there was insufficient evidence to prosecute the suspects. The victim's sister wants to know if a prosecution can be brought against the suspects by other means.
ask: Which option best advises the sister of the victim?

options.en: Only the Crown Prosecution Service can bring a criminal prosecution
The victim's sister may bring a private prosecution if she can show that the CPS's decision not to prosecute was 'unsafe'
The victim's sister may bring a private prosecution, subject to the Director of Public Prosecution's discretion
The victim's sister may bring a private prosecution, subject to the discretion of a High Court judge
The victim's sister may bring a private prosecution, subject to the Justice Minister's discretion

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is the best option. The victim's sister may bring a private prosecution, subject to the Director of Public Prosecution's discretion. There is an exception to the Crown bringing an action, where the prosecution is instigated by a private individual; namely a private prosecution. Section 6(1) of the Prosecution of Offences Act 1985 ("the Act") recognises the right of a private person to institute and conduct a private prosecution where the duty of the Director of Public Prosecutions ("the DPP") to take over them does not apply. But the right is subject to s.6(2) of the Act which confers upon the DPP a power, even when not under a duty to take over the proceedings, nevertheless to do Prosecutions ("the DPP") to take over them does not apply. But the right is subject to s.6(2) of the Act which confers upon the DPP a power, even when not under a duty to take over the proceedings, nevertheless to do so at any stage. In determining whether to do so, it is the DPP's policy to apply certain criteria, including in particular a criterion relating to the strength of the evidence in support of the prosecution. The DPP has a discretion so as to intervene and discontinue a prosecution if the private prosecution lacks a reasonable prospect of success. Statute; Rule; Constitution: Section 6(1)-(2) Prosecution of Offences Act 1985 (POA).

stem: An owner of a freehold property grants a parol lease of the property to a woman for three years. The woman does not intend to move into the property for six months after the beginning of the lease, as she is working abroad. Three months after granting the lease, the owner sells the property to a man, with vacant possession. The sale triggers compulsory first registration.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

The man will only be bound by the lease if he had actual notice of it
The man will only be bound by the lease if it was registered as a Land Charge

The man will not be bound by the lease

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. A lease for seven years or less ranks as an overriding interest which will override first registration of a legal estate, despite not being registered.

stem: A tenant leased a property from a landlord for 10 years in 2005 at a rent of £1,500 per calendar month (PCM). By 2008, due to worldwide recession, the tenant was struggling to pay the full amount of rent owed, so the landlord agreed an arrangement to reduce the rent to £750 PCM. This arrangement continued until the recession officially ended in 2010, whereupon the landlord served notice in January 2011 for a return to the original terms of the agreement, and also for the balance of the rent discounted during the recession.
ask: Which of the following statements best advises the parties with regard to promissory?

In these circumstances, the doctrine of promissory estoppel suggests that the landlord is entitled to recover the full rent from the end of the recession, but not the balance for the recession years

In these circumstances, the doctrine of promissory estoppel suggests that the landlord is not entitled to recover the full rent from the end of the recession, but would be able to recover the balance for the recession years

In these circumstances, the doctrine of promissory estoppel suggests that the landlord is entitled to recover the full rent from the end of the recession, the balance for the recession years, and the balance of the interest which had accrued

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. In these circumstances, the doctrine of promissory estoppel suggests that the landlord is entitled to recover the full rent from the end of the recession, but not the balance for the recession years. stem: The Monarch is deeply concerned about the escalation of the situation in a Middle East country. The government of the day is minded to commence military operations in the region against the country. The Monarch has personal reservations about this.

Although a Constitutional Monarch remains politically neutral, he or she retains the right to appoint the Prime Minister and to grant regular audiences during the Prime Minister's term of office. stem: The UK government has started to impose a charge on goods as they arrive into the country. As a result of interrupting the flow of goods, the UK government says that it is able to produce statistics which are made available to traders. The UK government argues that the charge imposed is therefore a payment for the benefit that the traders receive in the form of the statistics. The European Commission argues that the UK government's measure is a 'charge having equivalent effect to a customs duty'. Which option best defines what
ask: is a 'charge having equivalent effect to a customs?

options.en: charge that relates to a general system of internal dues applied, systematically and in accordance with, the same criteria to domestic products and imported products alike

A charge having equivalent effect to a customs duty is defined as any pecuniary • charge, if it constitutes payment for a service in fact rendered to the economic operator of a sum in proportion to the service

A charge having equivalent effect to a customs duty is defined as any pecuniary • charge if, subject to certain conditions, it attaches to inspections carried out to fulfil obligations imposed by EU law

A charge having equivalent effect to a customs duty is defined as any pecuniary charge which distorts or threatens to distort competition by favouring certain undertakings or the production of certain goods, insofar as it affects trade between Member States, incompatible with the internal market

A charge having equivalent effect to a customs duty is defined as any pecuniary charge, however small and whatever its designation and mode of application, which is imposed unilaterally on domestic or foreign goods by virtue of the fact that they cross a frontier

explanation.en: E is correct. According to constant case law, any pecuniary charge, however small and whatever its designation and mode of application, which is imposed, unilaterally, on goods by reason of the fact that they cross a frontier and which is not a customs duty in the strict sense, constitutes a charge having equivalent effect, under Article 30 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union Lead case: Case 24/68 Commission v Italy.

stem: The (fictitious) EU Bill recently received its second reading in the House of Lords. The Minister of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Office published the government's response to a report by the House of Lords Select Committee on the Constitution on the EU Bill the next day.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the role of Select Committees?

The primary function of a Departmental Select Committee is to scrutinise and investigate the activities of a particular government department

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. The primary function of a Departmental Select Committee is to scrutinise and investigate the activities of a particular government department. Parliament's select committees exist to investigate various aspects of public policy and society. Their work involves calling witnesses with expertise and experience in the field of the inquiry and they will often produce reports. stem: In order to improve the water supply to his mill, a mill owner employed an independent contractor to construct a reservoir on his land. stem: A woman and a man are cohabitees who purchase a freehold residential property. The property is registered in the man's sole name for tax purposes, but before they acquire it they agree that the property will belong to both of them. They live in the property for a number of years, with the man working to earn a salary which is used to pay the mortgage, and the woman staying at home to look after the children.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The man is the sole legal and beneficial owner of the property
The man holds the property on resulting trust for himself and the woman
The man holds the property on a constructive trust for himself and the woman
The man holds the property on resulting trust for the woman
The man holds the property on constructive trust for the woman

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. The man holds the property on a constructive trust for himself and the woman. Although the man has contributed to the whole of the purchase price of the property and the mortgage payments, it would be unconscionable for him to deny the woman an interest in the property since they had previously agreed between themselves that she would take an interest. In the absence of any specific contributions upon which to quantify the woman's interest, the equitable maxim that "equity delights in equality" would apply and the parties would be deemed to have equal beneficial entitlement to the property.

stem: A woman rents a commercial property from a man. The woman has fallen into arrears with her rent and the man wishes to enter the property to remove goods to the value of the rent owed.

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Where a landlord wishes to levy Commercial Rent Arrears Recovery (CRAR), they do not need a court order. stem: Your firm is on the panel for an insurance company on a standing retainer. You receive a new claim in which you are instructed by the insurance company to represent the interests of their policyholder.

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. You do not need to perform any customer due diligence. stem: The Magna Carta (Latin for "Great Charter") is one of the most celebrated documents in English history. stem: ICUIGIC EGGUMULA A Lord Justice reversed a Justice's decision regarding a contractual dispute between two parties. It later transpired that the Lord Justice had accepted a bribe from the party whom he found for on appeal. He is now facing calls for his removal.

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. Removal of a senior judge requires a resolution of both Houses of Parliament. stem: On 5 January, a man told his friend that he would be minded to buy the friend's car if it had had just one previous owner. Which of the following statements best describes how the friend's assertion about the car would affect the parties' position? Triend nad told him the car had nad only one previous owner; in tact there nad been 3 previous owners. There was no written contract.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes how the friend's assertion about the car would affect the parties' position?

options.en: The lapse of 24 hours between the making of the statement and the contract's conclusion would militate against construing the statement as a representation
The lapse of 24 hours between the making of the statement and the contract's conclusion would not militate against construing the statement as a contractual term
The lack of a written contract would militate against construing the statement as a representation
The lack of a written contract brings the doctrine of collateral contract into play, thus circumventing the so-called 'parol evidence rule'

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. The lapse of 24 hours between the making of the statement and the contract's conclusion would not militate against construing the statement as a contractual term. stem: A girl went to her boyfriend's house, believing he would not mind her breaking in. Being drunk, however, she broke the window of the wrong house.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the girl's criminal liability, if any?

options.en: A charge of criminal damage would be appropriate in these circumstances

The girl's belief that her boyfriend would consent only had to be genuine, regardless of whether her belief was reasonable

explanation.en: E is correct. The girl's belief that her boyfriend would consent only had to be genuine, regardless of whether her belief was reasonable. It is irrelevant when claiming a lawful excuse as to whether or not the belief was justified, provided it was honestly held. The belief that protection is necessary is a subjective test. Therefore, provided the defendant believes that the defence is applicable, this would be accepted. Lead case: Jaggard v Dickinson [1980]. Statute; rule; constitution: S. 5(2) Criminal Damage Act 1971.

stem: A sole trader whose business has run into financial difficulty knows that her business creditors plan to file for her bankruptcy. She has a large amount of equity in her home and, in order to place this out of the reach of her creditors, she transfers it to her friends to be held on trust for her during her lifetime, whereupon it should pass to her daughter.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The sole trader has created a valid trust and her home would not be available to her creditors
The trust would fail for lack of certainty of intention
The trust would fail for lack of certainty of objects
The trust would fail for lack of certainty of subject matter
The trust would fail for the lack of all three certainties

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. The trust would fail for lack of certainty of intention. Certainty of objects and subject matter exists in this situation. The relevant words indicating an intention to create a trust were included in the trust instrument. However, these words are only used to infer an intention to create a trust and should not be regarded as conclusive proof of such an intention. Therefore, if it can be shown that, notwithstanding the wording of the instrument, there was in fact no intention to create a trust, then the trust will be regarded as a sham and will fail for lack of certainty of intention.

stem: A woman has mortgaged a residential freehold property to a bank. The legal date for redemption was two months after the grant of the mortgage, which was granted three years ago. She wishes to redeem the mortgage.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The woman has no right to redeem the mortgage, as the redemption date has passed
The woman has a legal right to redeem the mortgage
The woman has an equitable right to redeem the mortgage
The woman has a legal right to redeem the mortgage on payment of the capital balance plus interest and costs
The woman has an equitable right to redeem the mortgage on payment of the capital balance plus interest and costs

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. The woman has an equitable right to redeem the mortgage on payment of the capital balance plus interest and costs. The woman's legal right to redeem the mortgage has been extinguished, as the legal redemption date has passed. However, the woman retains an equitable right to redeem the mortgage ("the equity of redemption"), provided that she pays the capital balance of the mortgage account, plus all accrued interest and costs, back to the mortgagee.

stem: A tenant entered in to a tenancy agreement with a local authority in regard to a block of flats. The agreement was silent as to who was to be responsible for the maintenance of the common areas of the block, and in particular the lifts and rubbish disposal units. The tenant is of the view that the local authority is contractually responsible by implication of a term.
ask: Which option best advises which implied term the tenant should plead?

options.en: The tenant should plead that there is a term implied by statute
The tenant should plead that there is a term implied by custom
The tenant should plead that there is a term implied in fact
The tenant should plead that there is a term implied by law
The tenant should plead that there is a term implied by description

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is the best option. The tenant should plead that there is a term implied by law. Occasionally, the courts imply a term that the parties would not, in fact, have considered. This is an instance where the courts imply as a matter of law how they think the contract should be performed. In Liverpool City Council v Irwin [1977] AC 239, the House of Lords spelt out that it was an implied term of the lease held by the council that the council should take reasonable care to maintain a property in a reasonable state of repair. This term will be implied into all contracts of the same nature as a matter of law.

A person is considered as a qualifying practitioner if he is an advocate in Scotland, or a solicitor entitled to appear in the Court of Session and the High Court of Justiciary, or is a member of the Bar of Northern Ireland or a solicitor of the Court of Court, Court of Appeal, Northern Irish High Court or Court of Appeal, or Scottish Court of Session) for a period of at least two years; or been a qualifying practitioner, for a period of at least 15 years (such as in this case). A person is considered as a qualifying practitioner if he is an advocate in Scotland, or a solicitor entitled to appear in the Court of Session and the High Court of Justiciary, or is a member of the Bar of Northern Ireland or a solicitor of the Court of Judicature of Northern Ireland. stem: A woman is the freehold owner of 123 The Street. The property is subject to a mortgage to the bank and the terms of the mortgage expressly exclude section 99 of the Law of Property Act 1925, by virtue of which a mortgagor is given the right to create a tenancy. The woman grants an assured shorthold tenancy of the property for 12 months to her friend. The woman subsequently falls behind on her mortgage payments and the bank exercises its power of sale, selling the property to a man.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The man is bound by the friend's tenancy
The man is only bound by the friend's tenancy if the bank consented to the tenancy being granted
The man is only bound by the friend's tenancy if he had notice of it
The man is not bound by the friend's tenancy whether or not the bank consented to it
The man is not bound by the friend's tenancy

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. The man is only bound by the friend's tenancy if the bank consented to the tenancy being granted. A purchaser from a mortgagee (exercising its power of sale) takes the property free from any encumbrances over which the mortgage has priority and subject to any encumbrances which have priority over the mortgage. The bank's mortgage will only be subject to the friend's tenancy if the bank consented to it being granted, and therefore if this is the case, the man will take the property subject to the friend's tenancy.

stem: A woman has been arrested for allegedly stealing a dress from a ladies fashion store. You are called to the police station to advise her prior to police interview. She is unsure what the police officer meant by the term "property" when he arrested her.
ask: Which of the following statements best defines the term "property" in regard to the?

options.en: "Property" includes money and all other property, real or personal, including things in action and other tangible property
"Property" includes land and all other property, real or personal, including things in action and other intangible property
"Property" includes goods and all other property, including things in action and other intangible property
"Property" includes money and all other property, real or impersonal, including things in action and other intangible property
"Property" includes money and all other property, real or personal, including things in action and other intangible property

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. E is correct. "Property" includes money and all other property, real or personal, including things in action and other intangible property. Theft deals with property and, in most cases, it is relatively clear whether or not property is being considered. One interesting point in the definition of property is that property extends to include both real and personal property and can also include intangible property. This has been held to mean that things that do not physically exist, such as debt, would be considered property, as would intellectual property rights, but confidential information would not (Oxford v Moss [1979] Crim LR 119).

stem: A man and woman purchase a house together. The land is registered in their joint names, but they do not include a declaration of trust in the transfer deed stating how the land is to be held. The man contributed 80% of the purchase price and the woman contributed the remaining 20%.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The two hold the property on trust for themselves as joint tenants in equal shares
The two hold the property on trust for themselves as joint tenants with 80% held by the man and 20% held by the woman
The two hold the property on trust for themselves as tenants in common in equal shares
The two hold the property on trust for themselves as tenants in common with 80% held by the man and 20% held by the woman
The man holds the property on trust for himself and the woman as tenants in common with 80% held by the man and 20% held by the woman

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. The two hold the property on trust for themselves as tenants in common with 80% held by the man and 20% held by the woman. Where the parties have contributed unequally to the purchase price of the property, equity will presume a tenancy in common in shares to reflect their contributions, unless a contrary intention is shown the transfer deed.

ask: Which of the following best describes the legal position?

options.en: Shareholders cannot enter into agreements with one another, unless it is signed by all the shareholders at the time of incorporation of the company
Shareholders can enter into agreements with one another
Only shareholders collectively holding over 50% of the shares can enter into agreements with one another
Shareholders can enter into agreements with one another providing the agreement is signed by 100% of the shareholders
Shareholders can enter into agreements without the majority shareholder if they receive the approval of the Financial Services Authority

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. Shareholders can enter into agreements with one another. In order to strengthen their position (s), minority shareholders can enter into shareholders agreements. This can protect their rights and enable them to enforce their rights against other shareholders and the company as a whole.

stem: Two sisters are appointed as the trustees of their late mother's modest will trust. The older sister has a highly paid job and is often travelling with work, whilst the younger sister, a housewife, if left to administer the affairs of the trust. The trust's assets are so small that it is not possible for the younger sister to instruct a solicitor to advise her. The younger sister misinterprets the terms of the trust deed and exercises the power of appointment in favour of a beneficiary who is not entitled to receive the capital. The beneficiary is the older sister's only son. The only other beneficiary of the trust is the younger sister's own son. Which of the following statements best describes the position should an action be brought by the beneficiary for breach of trust? ot appointment in tavour of a beneticiary who is not entitled to receive the capital. The beneficiary is the older sister's only son. The only other beneficiary of the trust is the younger sister's own son.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position should an action be brought by the beneficiary for breach of trust?

options.en: The older sister is not liable, as she was not involved in the affairs of the trust, and the younger sister is not liable, because she acted honestly and reasonably
The two sisters would both be liable, but the older sister could claim an indemnity from the younger sister, because the older sister was not involved in the affairs of the trust
The two sisters would both be liable
Only the older sister would be liable, because she was not involved in the affairs of the trust, whereas the younger sister acted honestly and reasonably
Only the younger sister would be liable, as she committed the breach of trust unilaterally, whereas the older sister was not involved in the affairs of the trust

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. The two sisters would be liable. The younger sister would still be liable for the breach of the terms of the trust regardless of whether she acted honestly and reasonably, as she has a duty to make herself aware of the terms of the trust. Although this could be viewed as a unilateral act by the younger sister, making her solely liable to the beneficiaries, or at least liable to indemnify the older sister under the rule in Head v Gould, the fact that the younger sister is not a professional trustee upon whose advice the older was entitled to rely means that the older sister is not entitled to an indemnity (see Bahin v Hughes (1886)).

stem: Of particular relevance to the discussion of murder cases is the mental element that exists within the defendant, as it is this that constitutes the fundament difference between manslaughter and murder.
ask: Intention is, therefore, crucial when it comes to Which of the following statements best defines the mens rea for murder?

options.en: The intent for murder is intention to kill or cause the victim to apprehend unlawful personal violence

The intent for murder is intention to kill or cause the victim to apprehend immediate and unlawful personal violence
The intent for murder is intention to kill or cause grievous bodily harm
The intent for murder is intention to kill or cause actual bodily harm

explanation.en: D is correct. For the principal defendant, the intent for murder is the intention to kill or cause grievous bodily harm, nothing less. Lead case: Lawrence v Metropolitan Police Commissioner (1972). View Results

stem: Whilst constitutional conventions are rules that are observed by the various constituted parts, they are not written in any document having legal authority. Nonetheless, it is very unlikely that there would be a departure of such conventions without good reason, even if an underlying enforcing principle has been overtaken by history, as these conventions also acquire the force of custom. Which of the following statements best describes the Ponsonby Rule? by history, as these conventions also acquire the torce of custom.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the Ponsonby Rule?

options.en: The Ponsonby Rule ensures that government ministers are responsible and can be held accountable for what happens in their departments

The Ponsonby Rule ensures that all government ministers, including the Prime Minister, must be members of the House of Commons or, the House of Lords, and are thereby accountable to the respective branches of the legislature

The Ponsonby Rule ensures that any treaty subject to ratification to be laid • before Parliament for at least 21 sitting days before ratification is carried out by the executive and that, in certain circumstances, such treaties will be debated
The Ponsonby Rule ensures that government Bills can get through the House of Lords when the government of the day has no majority in the Lords

The Ponsonby Rule ensures that requires a published code of conduct for the • civil service and sets out some minimum requirements for the code (including obligations of political impartiality, integrity, honesty, etc...)

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. The key features of the Ponsonby Rule (established by Arthur Ponsonby, Parliamentary Under-Secretary for Foreign Affairs, in 1924) are the publication of a treaty as a Command Paper and the laying of the Command Paper before both Houses of Parliament for at least 21 sitting days before ratification. stem: The European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) has, on occasion, pronounced that the very finding of a violation of a person's human rights is sufficient just satisfaction for non-pecuniary damages. However, on other occasions it has ordered monetary compensation, and has occasionally concluded that an alternative form of redress is most appropriate, particularly where there are continuing violations. Which of the following statements best describes the law relating to damages according to the principles established by the ECtHR?
ask: nich ot the tollowing statements best describes the law relating to damages according to the principles established by the ECtHR?

options.en: The ECtHR conducts its assessment of what an applicant is entitled to by way of • just satisfaction in accordance with the principles laid down in customary international law
The ECtHR conducts its assessment of what an applicant is entitled to by way of • just satisfaction in accordance with the principles or scales of assessment used by domestic courts
The ECtHR conducts its assessment of what an applicant is entitled to by way of • just satisfaction in accordance with the principles laid down in the internal law of the High Contracting Party
The ECtHR conducts its assessment of what an applicant is entitled to by way of just satisfaction in accordance with the principles laid down in its case law
The ECtHR conducts its assessment of what an applicant is entitled to by way of • just satisfaction in accordance with the principles laid down by domestic courts and in its own case law

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. The European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) conducts its assessment of what an applicant is entitled to by way of just satisfaction in accordance with the principles laid down in its case law. It does not conduct its assessment by any reference to the principles or scales of assessment used by domestic courts.

stem: A woman wishes to sell her shares in a private limited company to her friend, but has been told by the board of directors that she is not allowed to do so.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: The board of directors must agree with a transfer in order for it to be valid
The board of directors must agree with a transfer in order for it to be valid, but only if the shares in question amount to 20% of the business or more
A shareholder is always free to transfer their shares as they wish
A shareholder is always free to transfer their shares as they wish, unless the terms contained within the articles of association stipulate otherwise
The board of directors must agree with a transfer in order for it to be valid, but only if the shares in question amount to 10% of the business or more

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. Generally, shareholders have a right to transfer their shares. However, this right is subject to any clauses in the articles which may stipulate certain conditions (i.e., who the shares can be transferred to etc.).

stem: A woman is the freehold owner of 123 The Street, a registered freehold property. She has granted a mortgage to a bank by way of a lease for term of years absolute for 3000 years. She wishes to grant a second mortgage to a separate mortgage company.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The woman cannot grant a second mortgage over the property, as she has already granted a mortgage to the bank
The woman could grant a mortgage to the mortgage company by way of a reversionary lease or by way of legal mortgage
The woman can only grant a mortgage to the mortgage company by executing • a charge by way of legal mortgage, which would be registered in the charges register
The woman can only grant an equitable mortgage to the mortgage company which would be protected by the deposit of her title deeds
The woman can only grant a mortgage to the mortgage company by executing a charge by way of legal mortgage, which would be registered as a Land Charge

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. The woman could either grant a mortgage to the mortgage company by way of a reversionary lease (i.e. one which is longer in term to that which she has granted to the bank) or she could execute a charge by way of legal mortgage. However, she does not have to execute a charge. The reversionary lease would be registered against her title ranking in priority to that granted to the bank.

stem: A man and woman who are not married are joint tenants of a property worth £750,000. When the man dies, his interest in the property will pass to the woman. He assumes, therefore, that his interest in the property will not be included in his estate for the purposes of Inheritance Tax (IHT).
ask: Advise the man regarding the current legal position?

options.en: As the interest passes to the surviving joint tenant, the man's interest in the property will not make up part of his estate
The man's interest will not make up part of his estate, provided that he has another property which will be included in his estate
The man's interest in the property cannot pass to the woman
Joint tenants are only required to pay IHT if the property value at the time of death is over £1 million
Despite the man's interest passing to the woman, the man's interest will still be subject to IHT

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Despite the man's interest passing to the woman, the man's interest will still be subject to IHT. According the rules of survivorship, the man's interest in the property will pass to the woman, so his interest in the property won't be part of his will for distribution purposes. However, his interest in the property will form part of his estate for IHT purposes.

stem: A girl at the age of 12 is the beneficiary of a trust of shares created by her aunt's will. The girl's parents are themselves very wealthy; nevertheless, they apply to the girl's trustees to pay them an allowance to contribute towards the girl's maintenance. The trust instrument does not alter the statutory power of maintenance.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The trustees have no power to pay any of the trust funds to the girl's parents in these circumstances
The trustees have no power to pay any of the trust funds to the girl's parents, because they have their own substantial income
The trustees can pay income or capital to the girl's parents at their discretion
The trustees can pay income only to the girl's parents at their discretion
The trustees can pay capital only to the girl's parents at their discretion

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. Section 31 of the Trustee Act 1925 allows the trustees to pay income for the maintenance of a minor beneficiary. Whilst the trustees must take into account the fact that the beneficiary's parents or guardians may be able to pay for the maintenance of the child themselves, they still have discretion as to whether to pay. In the case of trusts or trust interests created or arising after 1st October 2014, the trustees are not required to have regard to this issue whatsoever.

stem: A man sold a garden to a woman, who agreed to covenant that she would maintain the garden's present condition and continue to allow individuals to enjoy it. The land was sold to a company which knew of the restriction contained in the contract between the man and the woman, but announced it was going to build on the garden. ask: would allow the man to prevent the company from building on its own?

options.en: company from building on its own land, because the company has acquired the property in good faith and cannot be restrained from doing any act just because its predecessor disagrees with it

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. stem: A Member of Parliament (MP) makes scathing allegations about the behaviour of a constituent during a debate; separately, they are accused of fiddling expenses. He claims parliamentary privilege as protection against consequences of both activities.
ask: Is the MP protected by Parliamentary privilege?

options.en: Yes, but that privilege is automatically waived in the case of defamation proceedings or criminal prosecutions

explanation.en: The best answer is E. Parliamentary privilege covers proceedings in Parliament, including whatever is said in debate, but not conduct such as false accounting. Parliamentary privilege covers two heads, one of which is freedom of speech, guaranteed by Article 9 of the Bill of Rights 1689, which states: "That the freedom of speech and debates or proceedings in Parliament ought not to be impeached or questioned in any court or place out of Parliament." This principle has been upheld even where an MP made allegations about the behaviour of a constituent during proceedings in Parliament - A v United Kingdom [2003] 36 EHRR 51. However, parliamentary privilege does not pose any bar to prosecuting MPs who are involved in fraud or debate, but not conduct such as false accounting. ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The man is the sole legal and beneficial owner of the property
The man holds the property on resulting trust for himself and the woman
The man holds the property on a constructive trust for himself and the woman
The man holds the property on resulting trust for the woman
The man holds the property on constructive trust for the woman

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. The man holds the property on a constructive trust for himself and the woman. The parties can demonstrate that there was on oral agreement between them prior to acquiring the property to the effect that they would both "own" the property, although it is registered in the man's name only. stem: A man and his friend are the directors of a private limited company. In the course of business, they secure an overdraft facility on the company's bank account. The friend offers a guarantee to the bank. The company goes into liquidation.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The bank can claim directly against the man, his friend and the company's members
The bank can claim directly against the man's friend and the company's members
The bank can claim directly against the man's friend to the extent of the guarantee and the company's members to the extent of their unpaid shares
The bank can claim directly against the man's friend to the extent of the guarantee
The bank can claim directly against the man and his friend

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. The bank can claim directly against the man's friend to the extent of the guarantee. A creditor will not normally have a right of redress against directors or members, even to the value of their unpaid shares, in a liquidation. Claims against members must be made by the liquidator. However, where a director or individual member provides a personal guarantee, the creditor may claim against the director or individual member directly.

stem: A freehold owner of a property has split it into two flats. In 1990, the freehold owner grants a lease of the downstairs flat to a man. The lease contains covenants: firstly, that the man and his successors in title will not commit waste on the property; and secondly, that they will not use the property for any purpose that will compete with the freehold owner's business. In 1996, the freehold owner transfers the freehold to a woman, and in 2000 the man assigns the lease to his friend.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The woman can enforce the first and second covenants against the man's friend
The woman can enforce the first covenant only against the man's friend
The woman can enforce the second covenant only against the man's friend
The woman can enforce the first and second covenants against the man and his friend
The woman can enforce the first covenant only against the man and his friend

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. The woman can enforce the first covenant only against the man's friend. As the lease was granted before 1996, the provisions of the Landlord and Tenant (Covenants) Act 1995 do not apply. As an assignee of the reversion, the woman does not enjoy privity of contract with anyone. She can, therefore, only enforce those covenants which touch and concern the land against those with whom she enjoys privity of estate. As the current assignee of the lease, this person is the man's friend. As only the first covenant touches and concerns the land, this is the only covenant that she can enforce against the man's friend.

stem: The European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention) sets out that courts must take into account the principles applied by the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) in relation to the award of compensation. If the ECtHR finds that there has been a violation of the Convention or the protocols, and if the internal law of the Member State concerned allows only partial reparation to be made, the court shall, if necessary, afford just satisfaction to the injured party. Which of the following best defines the meaning of 'protocol' in respect of the nas been a violation of the Convention or the protocols, and it the internal law of the Member State concerned allows only partial reparation to be made, the court shall, if necessary, afford just satisfaction to the injured party.
ask: Which of the following best defines the meaning of 'protocol' in respect of the?

options.en: A protocol to the Convention is a text which adds one or more rights to the original Convention or amends certain of its provisions
A protocol to the Convention is a remedy which adds one or more rights to the original Convention or amends certain of its provisions
A protocol to the Convention is a treaty which adds one or more rights to the original Convention or amends certain of its provisions
A protocol to the Convention is a statute which adds one or more rights to the original Convention or amends certain of its provisions
A protocol to the Convention is a text which adds one or more rights to the original Convention or ratifies certain of its provisions

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. A protocol to the Convention is a text which adds one or more rights to the original Convention or amends certain of its provisions. Those Protocols, that have been signed and ratified by the UK, or which have been signed with a view to ratification, amend the ECHR and can be enforced in UK law. Unless they are properly consented to, no claim can be made to the ECtHR against the UK Government under the Protocols. As of January 2010, fifteen protocols to the Convention have been opened for signature. These can be divided into two main groups: those changing the machinery of the Convention; and those adding additional rights to those protected by the Convention. The former require unanimous ratification before coming into force, while the latter are optional protocols, which only come into force between ratifying Member States (normally after a small threshold of states has been reached). Note: Once ratified, a protocol becomes an integral part of the European Convention on Human Rights ("the Convention"), having the same legal force as the main Convention. However, by their nature, protocols are often in the form of subsequent amendments or additions to the main Convention. Therefore, national governments are not always obliged to ratify a particular protocol even though they have obligations under the main Convention. For instance the British Government refused to ratify protocol 12 (regarding discrimination under national law) but was still bound to the terms of the main Convention. In this respect, since a protocol, unlike the main Convention does not confer an automatic free-standing right on citizens of signatory nations, it would not be correct, to describe a protocol as a Treaty, just as it would not be correct to describe an Article as a Treaty. Accordingly option C is not the best answer.

stem: Two directors of a private limited company are seeking a written resolution from the members of the company in order to remove a director from his post before the end of his term. The director in question believes the resolution must be a special resolution and passed at a meeting of the members, rather than by a written resolution. The articles of association of the company are silent as to the ways directors can be removed from their office before the end of their term. Which of the following best describes the legal position? resolution. The articies of association of the company are silent as to the ways directors can be removed from their office before the end of their term.
ask: Which of the following best describes the legal position?

options.en: A resolution to remove a director is a special resolution and must be passed a meeting
A resolution to remove a director is a special resolution but can be passed by a written resolution
A resolution to remove a director is an ordinary resolution, unless the company's articles of association state otherwise, and can be passed by a written resolution
A resolution to remove a director is an ordinary resolution, unless the company's articles of association state otherwise, and can be passed in a meeting or by a written resolution
A resolution to remove a director is an ordinary resolution according to the Companies Act and cannot be passed by a written resolution

explanation.en: E is the best answer. A resolution to remove a director is an ordinary resolution according to the Companies Act and cannot be passed by a written resolution. Generally, a resolution is an ordinary resolution unless the company's articles of association state that a higher majority is required than in an ordinary resolution. However, there are some instances in which the Companies Act 2006 (the Act) states that certain decisions by the members are considered to be ordinary resolutions or special resolutions. When the Act states that an ordinary resolution is required - such as a resolution to remove a director before the expiration of his period of office (section 168 of the Companies Act) - this is applicable despite any ordinary resolutions or special resolutions. When the Act states that an ordinary resolution is required - such as a resolution to remove a director before the expiration of his period of office (section 168 of the Companies Act) - this is applicable despite any requirements of a higher majority being made by the company's articles. The Act requires that a special notice will be given to the company at least 28 days before the meeting at which the decision to remove the director is moved. The Act also states that a resolution of a private company to remove a director or auditor before the expiration of their term in office may not be passed as a written resolution (section 288 of the Companies Act).

stem: A man decides to lease some commercial land and charges VAT on the rental income. The tenants complain that the renting of commercial land is exempt from VAT and that it cannot be charged.

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Renting commercial land can be exempt from VAT, but the landlord can choose to charge VAT if they wish to do so. Where renting commercial land is exempt from VAT, the landlord is also precluded from claiming input tax on his or her expenses, thus becoming the ultimate consumer who bears the tax. stem: Your client wishes to create a trust by which he leaves the property on trust in his will, but communicates the terms to a trustee privately. nat are the requirements of a halt-secret trust!
ask: What are the requirements of a half-secret trust?

options.en: The testator must intend to create a trust; communicate that intention to the trustee at any point and the trustee must accept
The testator must intend to create a trust and communicate that intention to • the trustee up to the execution of the will; that will be sufficient to establish a half-secret trust

The testator must intend to create a trust; communicate that intention to the trustee at any point up to the execution of the will and the trustee must accept, encouraging the testator to bequeath the money or property on the faith that the testator's intention will be carried out

The testator must intend to create a trust; communicate that intention to the trustee only after execution of the will and the trustee must accept, encouraging the testator to bequeath the money or property on the faith that the testator's intention will be carried out
A half-secret trust is not permissible; the trust and its terms must be communicated in full in the will

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. The testator must intend to create a trust; communicate that intention to the trustee at any point up to the execution of the will and the trustee must accept, encouraging the testator to bequeath the money or property on the faith that the testator's intention will be carried out. These elements were set out in Blackwell v Blackwell [1929] AC 318.

stem: After learning of plans to build a new toxic waste landfill site in their town, the residents decided to hold a public meeting. One resident proposes to the 80 residents present that they should all march immediately to the proposed site in order to gain more publicity for their protest.
ask: Which is the most relevant statement to the above scenario regarding restrictions, if any, that may be imposed on the proposed march?

options.en: There is a requirement to give the police notice of the march, because the purpose of the march is to demonstrate support for or opposition to the views of any person or body of persons
There is a requirement to give the police notice of the march, because the purpose of the march is to publicise a cause or campaign
There is a requirement to give the police notice of the march, because the purpose of the march is to mark or commemorate an event
There is a requirement to give the police notice of the march, because there is likely to be a minimum number of two participants
There is no procedural power to impose conditions on public processions in the UK

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. There is a requirement to give the police notice of the march, because the purpose of the march is to publicise a cause or campaign. The organiser in the vast majority of marches (i.e., public processions) will be required to inform the police concerning the march. Specifically, notice should be given to the police if the march is intended to: (1) demonstrate support for or oppositions to the views of any group; (2) publicise a cause or campaign; or (3) mark or commemorate an event. Notice is not required if the march is purely spontaneous or if it is for a funeral procession. Statute; rule; constitution: s. 11 Public Order Act 1986.

stem: GIL UNUS A man had sold his friend a laptop, and a few days later, promised his friend that the laptop was free of viruses.
ask: After using the laptop, the friend found it contained Is the man's promise enforceable?

options.en: The man's promise is enforceable and the friend would be able to recover • damages, because both parties must have contemplated that the laptop would be free of viruses
The man's promise is enforceable, because his representation in fact contained an implied promise that the laptop was sound
The man's promise is unenforceable, because his promise was made only after the sale, so there was no consideration
The man's promise is unenforceable, because courts are equitably bound to ensure such promises are enforced in these circumstances
The man's promise is enforceable; if that had been a true representation of the facts, then it would have constituted a binding contract

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. The man's promise is unenforceable, because his promise was made only after the sale, so there was no consideration. The friend is unable to sue on this promise, since the fact pattern does not state the man has provided any consideration for it. Lead case: Roscorla v Thomas (1842) 3 QB 234.

stem: A local authority negligently approved plans for the construction of a house which had defective foundations. The local authority concedes that the survey was negligent, but asserts that there was no damage to other property or to any person. Which of the following statements best describes the local authority's liability in negligence, if any, for conducting the negligent survey?
ask: which of the tollowing statements best describes the local authority's liability in negligence, if any, for conducting the negligent survey?

options.en: Since there is a sufficient relationship of proximity between the parties, such that the local authority ought to have reasonably contemplated that carelessness on its behalf would be likely to cause damage, the loss is recoverable
Since there is proximity between the parties, and there are no apparent grounds for limiting the scope of the duty owed, the loss is recoverable
Since there was neither damage to the other property nor to any person, the loss was only economic and, therefore, not recoverable
Since there is no liability for damage to other property or persons caused by latent defects, then where the loss is only economic, such as in these circumstances, it is not recoverable
Since there was foreseeability and proximity, the local authority owes a duty of care and is liable in negligence, unless there are policy reasons for holding that no duty existed

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. Since there was neither damage to the other property nor to any person, the loss was only economic and, therefore, not recoverable. There is no liability in tort for pure economic loss, and although there is potential liability for damage to other property or person caused by latent defect, the scenario states that this did not occur in this case. Lead case: Murphy v Brentwood District Council [1991].

stem: Families of two Afghani civilians killed by British armed forces in Afghanistan began judicial review proceedings in England. They claimed that the UK Government had violated their relatives' right to life under the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention) by failing or refusing to conduct independent inquiries into their relatives' deaths. Civilian 1 had been killed in cross-fire in the streets of Kandahar; civilian 2 had been killed unlawfully whilst in custody at a British military detention centre which was under effective British military control.
ask: Did the UK Government have jurisdiction under the Convention over the deceased Afghani civilians?

options.en: The civilians were not within the jurisdiction of the UK for the purposes of the Convention, because it would be absurd if an essentially European Convention could confer rights upon citizens of Afghanistan which are enforceable against the UK Government in the courts of England and Wales
Civilian 2 was not within the jurisdiction of the UK for the purposes of the • Convention when he was killed, but civilian 1 was within UK jurisdiction for Convention purposes when he was killed
Both civilian 1 and civilian 2 were within UK jurisdiction for Convention purposes when they were killed
Neither civilian 1 nor civilian 2 were within UK jurisdiction for Convention purposes when they were killed
Civilian 1 was not within the jurisdiction of the UK for the purposes of the • Convention when he was killed, but civilian 2 was within UK jurisdiction for Convention purposes when he was killed

explanation.en: E is correct. Civilian 1 was not within the jurisdiction of the UK for the purposes of the Convention when he was killed, but civilian 2 was within UK jurisdiction for Convention purposes when he was killed. It is sufficient if the "person" remains under the jurisdiction of the contracting State being complained against when the alleged violations happened, or are threatened. Article 1 of the ECHR states that parties must secure to everyone within their jurisdiction the rights defined in the ECHR. stem: A husband is the freehold owner of a property at 123 The Street and executes a transfer of his legal and equitable title to the property in favour of his wife, for no consideration. After the wife has registered the transfer and becomes the owner, the husband claims that he did not intend to make an outright gift to his wife and argues that she holds 123 The Street on trust for him. He is unable to adduce any evidence that he did not intend to make a gift. Which of the following statements best describes the position? consideration. After the wite nas registered the transter and becomes the owner, the husband claims that he did not intend to make an outright gift to his wife and argues that she holds 123 The Street on trust for him. He is unable to adduce any evidence that he did not intend to make a gift.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The wife is the absolute owner of 123 The Street and does not hold the property on trust for her husband, because the presumption of advancement applies
The wife holds the property on trust for her husband on an automatic resulting trust, as he did not make a declaration of trust
The wife holds the property on trust for the husband on a presumed resulting trust, as the transfer was voluntary and at nil consideration
The wife holds the property on trust for the husband on a presumed resulting trust, because the presumption of advancement does not apply
The wife holds the property on trust for the husband on an automatic resulting trust, because of the failure of an express trust

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. The wife is the absolute owner of 123 The Street and does not hold the property on trust for her husband, because the presumption of advancement applies. The presumption of advancement would apply, because the husband and wife are married (Tinker v Tinker (1970)) and, therefore, unless the presumption was rebutted by evidence to the contrary, a resulting trust would not be presumed and a gift would be presumed to have been made to the wife by her husband.

stem: The articles of association of a company provide that its business is the production of newspapers, and that the company has the power to borrow money and invest in new technology to further its business. The company's board of directors resolve that, in order to arrest the decline in the company's fortunes, the company should switch to an exclusively online format. Accordingly, the directors enter into contracts on the company's behalf to: secure a loan agreement with a bank and with a technology provider to purchase an online platform for its news service. Which option best advises a minority shareholder of the company who questions the validity of the two contracts? in order to arrest the decline in the company's tortunes, the company should switch to an exclusively online format. Accordingly, the directors enter into contracts on the company's behalf to: secure a loan agreement with a bank and with a technology provider to purchase an online platform for its news service.
ask: Which option best advises a minority shareholder of the company who questions the validity of the two contracts?

options.en: The two transactions are neither valid nor binding, because a company can only do what it is empowered to by its constitutional documents
The company has acted ultra vires (beyond its powers) and therefore, the transactions are void and unenforceable
Where an act is done contrary to any specific restriction, such as in this case, its validity can be questioned on the ground of lack of capacity
A shareholder who disagrees with an action outside the company's objects can sue the directors for any loss

explanation.en: E is the best option. No act, for example a contract, can be questioned on the basis of a lack of capacity in the company's constitution. Consequently, from an external perspective, the contracts between the company and the bank and the technology provider are valid and enforceable. Statute: Section 39 Companies Act. stem: A man planted a bomb under a car, and the subsequent explosion destroyed the car and resulted in the death of the driver. You are called to the police station to advise him prior to police interview. The man explains that he was acting according to instructions by local gangsters, who told him that they had kidnapped his wife and children and they would be killed unless he planted the bomb.
ask: Which of the following best states the man's defence, if any, to any criminal liability for murder arising from his actions?

options.en: The man would not have a defence to murder under these circumstances, because duress is not a defence to a charge of murder
The man would not have a defence to murder under these circumstances, • because no reasonable person would have been likely to have acted in the same way

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. Duress is not a defence to a charge of murder or attempted murder. stem: A retail company is looking for new suppliers and a potential supply company has actively promoted its interest in working with them. A manager at the supply company has offered a director of the retail company various gifts including holidays, club memberships and admission to high profile events. The director is concerned that acceptance of these gifts will conflict with his duties as a director.
ask: Which, if any, of the director's duties would be in question?

options.en: The duty to act within his powers
None. The director is only required to have a general goodwill towards the company
The duty to promote the success of the company and the duty not to accept benefits from third parties
The duty to avoid conflicts of interest
The duty to avoid conflicts of interest and the duty not to accept benefits from third parties

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. The duty to avoid conflicts of interest and the duty not to accept benefits from third parties. The Companies Act 2006 introduced a framework for directors. Within this framework there are seven duties by which directors must abide. Many of these refer to their conduct in relation to their own company (i.e., duty to act within their power, duty to promote the success of the company etc) and some are concerned with their conduct relating to other businesses. The duty not to accept benefits from third parties means that a director cannot accept anything from a third party by reason of his being a director or because of actions or decisions he may take due to being a director. There is also a duty to avoid a conflict parties means that a director cannot accept anything from a third party by reason of his being a director or because of actions or decisions he may take due to being a director. There is also a duty to avoid a conflict of interest. This can apply to transactions with third parties and means that a director must avoid situations in which he has an interest that conflicts with the company. In this instance, it's arguable that the supply company is offering the gifts in order to advance their own interests and that the director is the recipient because of his position in the company. If true, this would violate the director's duty not to accept benefits from third parties and is likely to impinge on his duty to avoid a conflict of interest.

stem: A fee simple owner of a house has divided it into flats, yielding a rental income of £600 per month. The owner agrees orally with her friend that he can occupy one of the flats on payment of £650 per month for one year, starting from the day that he and his new wife return from their honeymoon in three months.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: The lease does not comply with the Law of Property Act 1925 (LPA) and does not operate at law
The lease complies with the LPA but does not operate at law
The lease does not comply with the LPA but operates at law
The lease complies with the LPA and operates at law
It is not possible to create a lease orally

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. The lease does not comply with Section 52 of the Law of Property Act 1925 and does not operate at law. Section 52 provides that a legal lease may be created orally, provided that it is at the best rent reasonably obtainable, does not require the payment of a premium and takes effect immediately as it is granted. The lease granted to the friend takes effect in the future and does not comply with these requirements. Accordingly, it will operate as an equitable lease only.

stem: A defendant breached its statutory duty in respect to carrying out the performance of its duties under an Act of Parliament. The only manner of enforcing performance provided is criminal prosecution.
ask: Counsel for the defendant asserts that under the general rule, 'where an Act creates an obligation, and enforces the performance in a specified manner, performance cannot be enforced in any other manner' Which option best states the classes of exception, if any, to this general rule?

options.en: Where the statute provides a specific means of enforcement, the presumption against actionability is subject to whether: (1) an analogous obligation has already been held by the courts to give rise to a civil action; or (2) was meant for the benefit of a particular class

Where the statute provides a specific means of enforcement, the presumption against actionability is subject to whether: (1) the statutory provision was designed for the benefit of a limited class of persons; or (2) the obligation concerned a specific and confined obligation

Where the statute provides a specific means of enforcement, the presumption against actionability is subject to whether: (1) the provision occurs in a statutory context where other obligations are likely to be actionable; or (2) was meant for the benefit of a particular class

Where the statute provides a specific means of enforcement, the presumption against actionability is subject to whether: (1) the statutory provision was designed for the benefit of a limited class of persons; or (2) was meant for the benefit of the public at large

Where the statute provides a specific means of enforcement, the presumption against actionability is subject to whether: (1) the statute itself prescribes a penalty; or (2) there was a breach of a statutory duty

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is the best option. Where the statute provides a specific means of enforcement, the presumption against actionability is subject to whether: (1) the statutory provision was designed for the benefit of a limited class of persons; or (2) was meant for the benefit of the public at large. On the issue of whether a civil remedy is available or not, the courts will consider matters such as whether: the statutory provision designed for the benefit of a limited class of persons, or is meant for the benefit of the public at large. In Lonrho Ltd and another v Shell Petroleum Co Ltd and another (No 2) Lord Diplock confirmed that: "... the question whether legislation which makes the doing or omitting to do a particular act a criminal offence renders the person guilty of such offence liable also in a civil action for damages at the suit of any person who thereby suffers loss or damage, is a question of construction of the legislation..." (at p. 183). Lord Diplock noted, however, that the presumption against actionability where the statute provides a specific means of enforcement, such as by criminal penalty, is subject to the following exceptions: (1) in respect to the true construction of the Act it is apparent that the obligation or prohibition was imposed for the benefit or protection of a particular class of individuals; and (2) where the statute creates a public riaht (i.e. a riaht to be enjoved by all those of *3 provides a specific means of enforcement, such as by criminal penalty, is subject to the following exceptions: (1) in respect to the true construction of the Act it is apparent that the obligation or prohibition was imposed for the benefit or protection of a particular class of individuals; and (2) where the statute creates a public right (i.e. a right to be enjoyed by all those of Her Majesty's subjects who wish to avail themselves of it) and a particular member of the public suffers a particular, direct, and substantial" damage other and different from that which has common to all the rest of the public.
