stem: A woman saw a 'for sale' sign outside her neighbour's house and offered to buy the house at the advertised price. The neighbour promised to sell the house, in return for the woman's promise to pay.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the type of contract, if any, that has?

options.en: The type of contract that has been formed is a contract by deed
The type of contract that has been formed is a formal contract
The type of contract that has been formed is a bilateral contract
The type of contract that has been formed is a unilateral contract
No contract has been formed, as the woman's offer was merely an invitation to treat

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. The type of contract that has been formed is a bilateral (or two-sided) contract. A bilateral contract is one where a promise by one party is exchanged for a promise by the other. A bilateral contract places obligations upon and grants rights to both parties since they involve an exchange of a promise for a promise. Both parties are bound to one another at the beginning as each party has promised to do something for the other party.

stem: It is a statutory offence to impersonate "any person entitled to vote" at a general election. He was acquitted of the relevant statutory offence, because the court held that the deceased was not "a person entitled to Which of the following statements best describes the rule of statutory interpretation applied by the court in the scenario? but who nad died betore the election.
ask: He was acquitted of the relevant statutory offence, because the court held that the deceased was not "a person entitled to Which of the following statements best describes the rule of statutory interpretation applied by the court in the scenario?

options.en: The rule of statutory interpretation applied by the court in the scenario is the golden rule
The rule of statutory interpretation applied by the court in the scenario is the literal rule
The rule of statutory interpretation applied by the court in the scenario is the mischief rule
The rule of statutory interpretation applied by the court in the scenario is the purposive approach

explanation.en: You did not select the best answer. B is the best answer. The rule of statutory interpretation applied by the court in the scenario is the literal rule. The literal rule of interpretation is that the intention of Parliament is to be found by giving the words their ordinary and literal meaning, i.e. so long as the words of an Act are clear, the court must follow them, even though they might lead to a "manifest absurdity". In the lead case of Whiteley v. Chappel (1868) the court held that a deceased person was not entitled to vote because a deceased person no longer existed and for that reason had no legal rights. stem: An adventure company is charged with employing unlicensed tour guides after a trekker was killed after falling from a mountain ledge.

A company may be criminally responsible for offences requiring mens rea through the de minimis principle
A company may be criminally responsible for offences requiring mens rea through the identification principle

explanation.en: E is the best option. A company may be criminally responsible for offences requiring mens rea by way of the identification principle ("the principle"). This is where "the acts and state of mind" of those who represent the directing mind will be imputed to the company limits the application of the principle to the actions of Board of Directors, Managing Directors and potentially other senior officers who perform management tasks and speak and act as the company. stem: Families of an Afghani civilian killed by British armed forces in Afghanistan began judicial review proceedings in England. They claimed that the UK Government had violated their relative's right to life under the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention) by failing or refusing to conduct an independent inquiry into his death. He had been killed unlawfully whilst in custody at a British military detention centre in Afghanistan which was under effective British military control.
ask: Would the Human Rights Act 1998 (HRA) apply outside the territory of the UK in such?

options.en: The HRA does not apply to this case, because it has no extra-territorial application outside the UK
The HRA will apply to what UK public authorities, such as the Army, do beyond UK shores in areas of effective British control

The HRA does not apply, because misdeeds by military personnel are already • triable and punishable under the service discipline statutes (such as court martials), no matter where the crime is committed or who the victim may be
The HRA applies in this scenario, because the UK Government is liable for • breaches under the HRA in Afghanistan, or anywhere else in the world, should anybody be minded to mount a claim

Absent a clear inference of extra-territorial application in the terms of the HRA, • the HRA does not apply, since it cannot be doubted that, if Parliament had intended it to have extraterritorial application, it would have expressly said so

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. The HRA will apply to what UK public authorities, such as the Army, do beyond UK shores in areas of effective British control. British jurisdiction would extend to the base in which the victim was detained, in the same way it does to embassies, and therefore Section 6 of the HRA, which mandates that it is unlawful for public authorities to act in a way that is incompatible with Convention Rights, applies in this case. Lead case: R (Mazin Mumaa Galteth Al Skeini and others) v Secretary of State for Defence [2007] UKHL 26.....•--sly said so 26. Comment: Convention Rights are not restricted to those who are citizens, domiciled or ordinarily residents in the national territory of the contracting State. It is sufficient that those who allege violation, or threatened violation, are within the control of the contracting State. The control being exercised, must be "effective control", which means that it must impact or, at least, inform the actual actions and omissions of the individual alleging violation or threatened violation. Statute; rule; constitution: Article 1 ECHR.

stem: A man executes a declaration of trust transferring £50,000 to a woman (a UK resident aged 17), a private limited company and to his friend (a Spanish resident aged 20) to be held on trust for a beneficiary until he attains the age of 25.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The woman, the company and the man's Spanish friend can all act as trustees and the trust is valid
The woman cannot act as a trustee, because she is a minor, but the trust is nevertheless valid
The woman cannot act as a trustee, because she is a minor and the company cannot act as a trustee, being a company, but the trust is nevertheless valid
The woman cannot act as a trustee, because she is a minor, and the company • cannot act as a trustee, being a company, and the trust is invalid as there would only be one trustee

The woman cannot act as a trustee, because she is a minor, the company cannot act as a trustee, being a company, and the man's Spanish friend cannot act as a trustee, because he is not resident in the UK and, therefore the trust is invalid

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. The woman cannot act as a trustee, because she is a minor, but the trust is nevertheless valid. A minor cannot act as a trustee (s.20 Law of Property Act 1925). However, there is no prohibition on companies to act as trustees. As for people who are not resident in the UK, Section 36(1) of the Trustee Act 1925 provides that where a trustee remains outside of the UK for more than 12 months, they can be replaced. In the case of Whitehead's Will Trusts [1971] 2 All ER 1334, the court held that the words of Section 36 'are not apt to prevent the appointment of a person residing out of the UK'. It is also said that appointment of a trustee who is not resident in the UK is voidable not resident in the UK, Section 36(1) of the Trustee Act 1925 provides that where a trustee remains outside of the UK for more than 12 months, they can be replaced. In the case of Whitehead's Will Trusts [1971] 2 All ER 1334, the court held that the words of Section 36 'are not apt to prevent the appointment of a person residing out of the UK'. It is also said that appointment of a trustee who is not resident in the UK is voidable (albeit not void), in the instance of the beneficiaries, unless there are grounds to believe that the appointment is for the benefit of the beneficiaries. The appointment of the company and the man's Spanish friend would, therefore, be valid, and the trust would be properly constituted.

stem: Your client is the mortgagee of a mortgage secured against commercial premises. The mortgagor is in breach of the terms of the mortgage and the mortgagee seeks immediate possession. The mortgage deed is silent on the issue of notice before repossession. Your client does not wish to give notice to the mortgagor as it anticipates physical fortification and resistance if the mortgagor is put on notice of intended repossession.
ask: Can your client take immediate possession of the mortgaged property without providing notice and what would the mortgagor's remedies be, if any?

options.en: Yes, your client has the right to immediate possession without notice, and the mortgagor has no remedy against this course of action
Yes, your client has the right to immediate possession without notice; the mortgagor can only sue where he has reasonable grounds for not complying with the terms of the mortgage deed
No, your client has no right of immediate possession, with or without notice; a mortgagor may sue for possession and recovery of rents or profits
No, your client may only take immediate possession of a mortgaged property with notice. The mortgagor may sue for possession and recovery of rents or profits
No, your client may only take immediate possession of a mortgaged property with notice. However, the mortgagor has no remedy against immediate position where this occurs without notice

explanation.en: •vithout You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. Generally speaking, a mortgagee is entitled to possession of the mortgaged property from the date that the mortgage is executed where the mortgage is silent on the issue (Four-Maids Ltd v Dudley Marshall (Properties) Ltd [1957] Ch 317). Where the mortgage provides that the mortgagee is only entitled to possession following a default by the mortgagor and upon prior notice to the mortgagor, then he must allow a reasonable period of time between the making of a demand and the taking of possession to allow the mortgagor to comply with the demand (Toms v Wilson (1863) 4B & S 442, Ex Ch.).

stem: An offer is faxed on Monday 5 September to company A from company B's Leeds office stipulating that any acceptance must be faxed by close of business Wednesday 7 September. Company A duly faxed acceptance to company B's Bristol office at 3.30pm Wednesday 7 September, although the contract itself was signed and dated 6 Which of the following statements best advises when, if at all, and where the acceptance took effect?

options.en: Acceptance took effect in Bristol 7 September, because a valid acceptance by fax takes effect from when it has been read by the offeror
Acceptance took effect in Leeds 7 September, because a faxed acceptance takes effect at the place where it is sent
Acceptance took effect in Leeds 6 September, because contracts take effect where they are signed and dated
Acceptance took effect in Bristol 7 September, because a faxed acceptance takes effect at the place where it is received

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. Acceptance took effect in Bristol 7 September, because a faxed acceptance takes effect at the place where it is received. Due to the nature of instantaneous means of communication, acceptance is effective when received, not when posted or when the contract was signed. Lead case: Entores v Miles Far East Corp.

stem: Your senior associate has had enough of the rudeness of your current client in a litigation matter. In addition, the client's constant demands for detailed updates, along with extremely high expectations as to the capability of the litigation team, are time-consuming to deal with. The senior associate seeks to terminate the retainer with the client immediately. Are these good enough reasons to terminate the retainer with the client litigation matter. In addition, the client's constant demands tor detalled updates, along with extremely high expectations as to the capability of the litigation team, are time-consuming to deal with. The senior associate seeks to terminate the retainer with the client immediately.
ask: Are these good enough reasons to terminate the retainer with the client?

options.en: No reasons are needed; the solicitor can terminate the retainer at any time, for any reason
No; these do not constitute good enough reasons to justify terminating the retainer
No reasons are needed to terminate a retainer, but a solicitor can only terminate a retainer on giving reasonable notice to the client
A solicitor may only terminate a retainer if the client is provided with alternative options to pursue their matter
A solicitor may never terminate their retainer with a client

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is B. No; these do not constitute good enough reasons to justify terminating the retainer. Whilst a client may terminate a retainer at any time, for any reason, you must not cease acting for a client except for good reason and on reasonable notice, and you must provide the client with alternative options to pursue their matter (IB1.10 and IB1.26). Good reasons include: • where the solicitor cannot act in the client's best interests (IB1.7); • where a conflict of interest arises, or where there is a significant risk of a conflict (03.4, 03.5 and IB1.12) • where the solicitor is unable, despite his best efforts, to obtain clear instructions from the client; -3 • where the client refuses to pay an interim sum on account of costs during contentious proceedings (after reasonable notice), or where there is an express agreement for such a sum in a non-contentions matter as a condition of accepting instructions - and this has not been made; • where the solicitor cannot continue to act without being in breach of the duty of confidentiality (04.4 and IB4.5); • where the solicitor cannot continue to act without being in breach of the law (mandatory Principle 7) or where the client requires him to perform some act which is unprofessional (e.g. to mislead the court (IB5.5): not to notifv all parties where there is a (IB5.5); not to notify all parties where there is a contract race (O11.3); not to notify the Legal Services Commission (formerly the Legal Aid Board) of inaccurate information furnished to it by the client); • where the client or the solicitor becomes bankrupt or suffers from mental incapacity; • where there is a serious breakdown in confidence between the solicitor and the client (e.g. where the solicitor has properly and correctly advised the client and the client refuses to follow the solicitor's advice). Once the retainer has been accepted it should not be terminated by a solicitor until the job in hand has been completed (otherwise the solicitor will be liable in Commission (formerly the Legal Aid Board) of inaccurate information furnished to it by the client); • where the client or the solicitor becomes bankrupt or suffers from mental incapacity; • where there is a serious breakdown in confidence between the solicitor and the client (e.g. where the solicitor has properly and correctly advised the client and the client refuses to follow the solicitor's advice). Once the retainer has been accepted it should not be terminated by a solicitor until the job in hand has been completed (otherwise the solicitor will be liable in damages, as well as being in breach of Rule 1 for failing to act in the client's best interests).

stem: You are involved in a conveyancing transaction in which you act for both the buyer and the buyer's parents, who are advancing the remainder of the purchase price. You received a £15,000 deposit from the buyer and the £135,000 balance of the purchase funds from the buyer's parents.
ask: Which of the following best reflects the correct reasoning and best accounting entries to process the money?

options.en: You must open separate client ledger accounts to record the monies received: Debit cash sheet client account (£15,000); Credit buyer's ledger client account (noting 'deposit') (£15,000); Debit cash sheet client account (£135,000); Credit buyer's parents' ledger client account (noting 'property purchase funds') (£135,000).

As the monies will be used to pay the seller, they are office monies and are paid into the office account: Debit cash sheet office account (£15,000); Credit buyer's ledger office account (noting 'deposit') (£15,000); Debit cash sheet office account (£135,000); Credit buyer's ledger office account (noting 'property purchase funds') (£135,000).

All monies received in connection with the transaction are held by you as stakeholder for the buyer and seller jointly. You would therefore record both payments, separately, in a stakeholder ledger account: Debit cash sheet client account (£15,000); Credit stakeholder ledger client account (noting 'deposit') (£15,000); Debit cash sheet client account (£135,000); Credit stakeholder ledger client account (noting 'property purchase funds') (£135,000).
You may record all the monies received in the buyer's ledger account as one lump sum: Debit cash sheet client account (£150,000); Credit buyer's ledger client account (£150,000).

You may record, separately, the monies in the buyer's ledger account, identifying the funds belonging to each client: Debit cash sheet client account (£15,000); Credit buyer's ledger client account (noting 'deposit') (£15,000); Debit cash sheet client account (£135,000); Credit buyer's ledger client account (noting 'property purchase funds') (£135,000).

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. Whilst you are acting for the borrower and the lender (the buyer and their parents), Rule 29.10 of the SRA Accounts Rules (the Rules) only allow you to use one client ledger account where the funds belong to each client and the lender is an institutional lender. The latter is clearly not the case here, so you cannot rely on this provision. Accordingly, you must record the monies in separate client ledger accounts, as they are, for accounting purposes, separate parties to whom the firm, on receipt of the monies, will owe liabilities. B is wrong because the monies constitute client money under Rule 12. Under Rule 14.1, client money must be paid into a client account, unless the relevant exemptions permitted by the Rules apply, which they do not here. Under Rule 29.2, all dealings with client money must be appropriately recorded in a client cash account. You would not be properly accounting for your dealings with the client money and would therefore be in breach of several Rules. C is wrong - you would not hold the balance of purchase funds as stakeholder, as they are paid in order to effect completion, as opposed to funds being held as stakeholder, to be paid to the seller on completion or returned to the buyer in the event that the deal falls through. through. D is wrong, because you are not properly accounting for your dealings with client monies, which were separate payments by separate parties. You would breach Rules 29.1 and 29.2. E is wrong, because it relies on the provision of Rule 29.10. As discussed when explaining why Answer A is correct, the parents will not be considered institutional lenders, so you cannot rely on this provision, and must therefore record the monies in separate client ledger accounts.

stem: EU finance ministers are deliberating a proposal from the European Commission to impose a tax on all bank transactions. The UK minister indicates that he will veto the proposal. The 'Eurozone' finance ministers intend to vote for the proposal. Which of the following statements best describes the system
ask: which will allow the Council of the European Union to use a majority, rather than unanimous voting nich ot the tollowing statements best describes the system wnich will allow the Council of the European Union to use a majority, rather than unanimous voting?

options.en: The system which will allow the Council of the European Union to use a majority, rather than a unanimous voting procedure, is called 'co-decision'
The system which will allow the Council of the European Union to use a majority, rather than a unanimous voting procedure, is called 'intergovernmental co-operation'
The system which will allow the Council of the European Union to use a • majority, rather than a unanimous voting procedure, is called the 'preliminary ruling procedure'
The system which will allow the Council of the European Union to use a • majority, rather than a unanimous voting procedure, is called 'enhanced co- operation'
The system which will allow the Council of the European Union to use a majority, rather than a unanimous voting procedure, is called 'double majority'

explanation.en: E is correct. The system which will allow the Council of the European Union to use a majority, rather than a unanimous voting procedure, is called 'double majority'. Majority voting, rather than unanimous decisions will become more common. From 1 November 2014 a new procedure for qualified majority voting applies in the Council. Under this procedure, when the Council votes on a proposal by the Commission or the High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, a qualified majority is reached if 2 conditions are met: - 55% of member states vote in favour - in practice this practice this means 16 out of 28 - the proposal is supported by member states representing at least 65% of the total EU population This new procedure is also known as the 'double majority' rule. Note, however, that qualified majority is still the most widely used voting method in the Council. It is used when the Council takes decisions during the ordinary legislative procedure, also known as co-decision.

stem: A chemical firm owns and operates a factory near to a predominantly rural area of a town, which manufactures components for the Royal Air Force (RAF). Over a long period local inhabitants have been complaining that the emissions from the factory fall as acid rain. This damages their washing which they hang out to dry on their washing lines in their gardens, and the nearby local authority owned football pitches they regularly used, making the surfaces unplayable. wnich may be avallable at common law to the local residents ot the town!
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the most appropriate action, if any, which may be available at common law to the local residents of the town?

options.en: The most appropriate action available to the local inhabitants of the town is to • bring an action in public nuisance for damage to the laundry and private nuisance for damage to the football pitches
The most appropriate action available to the local inhabitants of the town is to bring an action in private nuisance for damage to the laundry and public nuisance for damage to the football pitches
The most appropriate action available to the local inhabitants of the town is to • bring an action in private nuisance for damage to the laundry and for damage to the football pitches
The most appropriate action available to the local inhabitants of the town is to bring an action in public nuisance for damage to the laundry and for damage to the football pitches

Although damage appears to have been caused, no action is available to the • local inhabitants of the town in either public or private nuisance because of the essential national function of supplying components to the RAF

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. The most appropriate action available to the local inhabitants of the town is to bring an action in private nuisance for damage to the residents' laundry and public nuisance for damage to the football pitch. In order for an action to sound in private nuisance, the residents must show a proprietary interest in the land affected by the nuisance. Injury to a person or a person's property is illustrative of private nuisance and this is an example of an industrial complex causing noxious emissions which causes damage to the residents' land. It seems clear in this scenario, that the residents either owned or occupied the land on which the damage was caused to their laundry. In terms of terms of the local authority owned football pitch, the residents do not appear to have a proprietary interest in the land. The likelihood is that, at most, the residents that use the pitches are mere licensees. However, to bring a claim under public nuisance in tort, unlike a claim in tort for private nuisance, the residents would not have to show that they had a legal interest in the land. It seems likely that the residents could establish the tort of public nuisance, since they are likely to be able to show they have been affected by the nuisance as particular class of the public. Lead case: Halsey v Esso Petroleum Co Ltd [1961].

stem: A man and his friend are the directors of a private company limited by shares, some of which are owned by family members. The company is in debt and the two directors are trying to source funds. They inform all shareholders that they will be required to pay an additional amount in order to clear the debt. The shareholders are reluctant to pay but are not sure if they can avoid it.
ask: Which of the following best describes the legal position?

options.en: The shareholders are required by law to pay towards clearing the debt
Only the majority shareholders must contribute additional funds
Shareholders can only be forced to pay additional funds if the company is wound up
Only shareholders that are family members and hold more than 50% of the shares can be forced to pay additional funds
Once shareholders have paid the full nominal value of their shares they cannot be forced to pay any further amounts

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Regardless of whether the company is in debt or has been 'wound up' shareholders are only required to pay the full nominal value of their shares and no more.

stem: A rich widow who is a big fan of fox hunting funds an annual hunt in her home town. The widow has executed a charitable purpose trust which is invalid

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is E. The widow has executed a non-charitable purpose trust which is invalid. There is no certainty of objects and, therefore, the trust will fail if it is not a charitable purpose trust unless it falls into one of the exceptions for non-charitable purpose trusts. The trust is not charitable as it does not fulfil the requirements of the Charities Act 2006. The promotion of foxhunting was previously one of the established exceptions to the rule against non-charitable purpose trusts. However, the rule that a purpose trust is invalid if it violates public policy, and the effect of the Hunting Act 2004, would mean that the trust would be held to be invalid.

stem: After learning of plans to build a new toxic waste landfill site in their town, the residents decided to organise a march against the proposed development. The following week, half-way through the march, at least 50 protestors decide to break away from the official main group and head towards the landfill site. Police officers confront the breakaway group and inform them that if they don't return to the main march, that they will be arrested for failing to comply with police conditions. With reference to the Public Order Act 1986 (the Act), which is the best advice to give to the breakaway marchers? contront the breakaway group and intorm them that it they don't return to the main march, that they will be arrested for failing to comply with police conditions.
ask: With reference to the Public Order Act 1986 (the Act), which is the best advice to give to the breakaway marchers?

options.en: The police officers may not lawfully confront the breakaway group, since no offence is being committed
The police officers may not lawfully confront the breakaway group, since no offence has been committed
The police officers may not lawfully confront the breakaway group, since no offence is about to be committed
The police officers may lawfully confront the breakaway group, because there is a specific power of arrest under the Act in relation to this offence
The police officers may lawfully confront the breakaway group, because offences are committed by those who organise, or take part in a march, and knowingly fail to comply with a condition

explanation.en: E is correct. The police officers may lawfully confront the breakaway group, because offences are committed by those who organise, or take part in a march, and knowingly fail to comply with a condition. Section 12 Public Order Act 1986 provides police with the power to impose conditions on processions "to prevent serious public disorder, serious criminal damage or serious disruption to the life of the community." This may include conditions as to the route to be followed, and may specify that the procession is not to enter a particular public place. Statute; rule; constitution: s. 12 Public Order Act 1986.
